analysts.analyst: occupation-mechanics (HoI4 La Resistance, Vic2/3, CK control, COIN-series & Vietnam '65 lens)

findings.title: Control and support are two different resources; the 'hold it but don't own it' feel comes from tracking both
findings.detail: The COIN board game series (Fire in the Lake, A Distant Plain) gets its entire texture from splitting map ownership into CONTROL (whose troops dominate the space) and SUPPORT/OPPOSITION (what the population wants). A city can be COIN-controlled while its population actively opposes the government, and shifting support requires sustained presence plus spent resources (Pacification), capped at slow per-turn rates, while a single enemy Terror action can undo months of work and leave a marker that must be cleared before support can rise again. Victory in these games is scored on support, not control, which is precisely why holding territory never feels solved. Any occupation system that collapses these into one number ('province -> occupier tag') has designed the feel away by construction. The minimum viable version is two per-zone tracks: military control (binary-ish, set by armies) and alignment/compliance (continuous, slow, expensive, reversible).
findings.evidence: GMT COIN series rules and reviews: Fire in the Lake rulebook (https://www.gmtgames.com/fireinthelake/FireLake-RULES-Final.pdf), PAXsims review noting control-vs-support as the core political layer (https://paxsims.wordpress.com/2014/10/10/review-fire-in-the-lake/), The Boardgames Chronicle COIN introduction (https://theboardgameschronicle.com/2023/02/12/introducing-coin-fire-in-the-lake/).

findings.title: HoI4's La Resistance rework: occupation became a choice of extraction strategy, and its stated purpose was to put a clock on conquest snowballing
findings.detail: Paradox's 1.9 rework replaced 'meet suppression number or eat sabotage' with three interacting dials: resistance (grows, causes sabotage/attrition), compliance (grows slowly, unlocks factories/resources/manpower from the occupied state), and occupation laws that explicitly trade among three objectives — compliance growth (long-term), resistance suppression (short-term safety), and immediate exploitation (short-term gain). Crucially, occupied territory yields far LESS than owned territory by default; you earn access back over years via compliance. The devs explicitly framed the rework as anti-snowball: conquest stops paying for itself immediately, world-conquest runs gain a clock. The collaboration-government spy operation is the standout idea for your intel pillar: an expensive COVERT investment made BEFORE/DURING the war that raises starting compliance and lowers the enemy's capitulation threshold — pre-war intelligence work literally purchases a cheaper occupation. The weakness: after picking a law, the system runs itself; garrisons are a template assignment, resistance is a passive attrition tax that almost never threatens anything strategically, so mid/late-game it degrades into a solved checkbox again.
findings.evidence: HoI4 Dev Diary — Resistance and Compliance (https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/hoi4-dev-diary-resistance-and-compliance.1240349/), EIP Gaming 1.9/La Resistance summary (https://eip.gg/hoi4/news/hearts-of-iron-iv-patch-1-9-new-intelligence-system-la-resistance-dlc/), StrateGGames resistance guide (https://old.strateggames.com/a/resistance-to-occupation-in-hoi4/).

findings.title: Victoria's answer: annexation is priced internally (turmoil + incorporation time) and externally (infamy), and the external price is the one that actually deters
findings.detail: Vic3 makes conquest expensive inside your own economy: fresh conquests carry high turmoil that cripples the very construction you need to fix it, unincorporated states suffer roughly -33% standard of living, -50% political strength, -50% conscription, and incorporation costs bureaucracy over time scaled by cultural distance (~27 months for same-culture, up to ~22 years for alien homelands). But the sharper Cold-War-relevant lesson is Vic2's infamy ('badboy'): every unjustified territorial grab adds to a visible international ledger, and past a threshold the whole world gains free cause for containment wars against you. Internal costs alone are payable by a rich player — they make annexation slow, not wrong. The external ledger is what makes 'transfer everything to me' a strategic act with a price the player cannot simply out-produce, because it is denominated in other actors' behavior. For a game whose failure state is total war, infamy naturally becomes escalation/tension: illegitimate conquest converts directly into the currency of the game's loss condition.
findings.evidence: Victoria 3 wiki on states/incorporation (https://vic3.paradoxwikis.com/State), StrateGGames post-conquest guide (https://old.strateggames.com/a/what-to-do-after-you-conquer-state-in-victoria-3/), Paradox forum thread on turmoil vs construction (https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/turmoil-decreasing-construction-efficiency-is-idiotic.1574071/), Victoria 2 infamy mechanics (long-standing badboy system, Paradox wikis).

findings.title: Occupation must draw from the same pool as the front line — the garrison IS the opportunity cost
findings.detail: Vietnam '65 works because every unit babysitting a village for hearts-and-minds is a unit not hunting the VC main force, and political points (the victory resource) pay for both operations and logistics — pacification and combat compete for one budget. HoI4's garrison demand similarly pulls real equipment and manpower from the shared pool, which is the only part of its resistance system players genuinely feel (bleeding thousands of rifles and trucks to partisans). CK-style control does the time version: after you take a holding, control climbs slowly and taxes/levies are throttled until it does. The design rule: never fund occupation from a dedicated 'occupation resource' that exists only for this purpose — fund it from the army, the treasury, and the political capital the player already wants for other things. In your Korea case this is automatic and beautiful: every division pinned on counter-guerrilla duty in the North Korean interior is a division missing from the Yalu line facing the PLA.
findings.evidence: Vietnam '65 reviews on the pacification/ops tension: Quarter to Three (https://www.quartertothree.com/fp/2015/03/19/in-the-shit-with-vietnam-65/), TouchArcade (https://toucharcade.com/2015/06/05/vietnam-65-review/), No Dice No Glory retrospective (https://nodicenoglory.com/retrospective-of-vietnam-65/); HoI4 garrison equipment-drain from the La Resistance dev diaries.

findings.title: Insurgency needs an external sponsor and a sanctuary, or it decays into a static tax
findings.detail: The COIN games and Vietnam '65 both model insurgency as externally FED: the Ho Chi Minh Trail, NVA infiltration, cross-border sanctuaries. Cut the feed and the insurgency starves; leave it and no amount of local suppression wins. This is what turns occupation into diplomacy: the level of resistance in your occupied zone is partly a dial held by your RIVAL, which makes it negotiable (a settlement can include the sponsor cutting support) and ties occupation directly to the intel pillar (their covert ops raise resistance in your zone; your counterintel and interdiction suppress the feed). HoI4 half-has this — enemy 'Boost Resistance' spy ops — but with no sanctuary geography it stays abstract. Historically this is exactly Korea: post-1953 North-sponsored infiltration into the South persisted for decades; an occupied North bordering an unreconciled PRC/USSR should never fully pacify.
findings.evidence: Fire in the Lake trail/infiltration mechanics (GMT rules/playbook, https://www.gmtgames.com/fireinthelake/FireLake-PLAYBOOK-Final.pdf); Vietnam '65's VC respawn from the trail as the core loop (Quarter to Three review); hearts-and-minds historical framing (https://history.state.gov/conferences/2010-southeast-asia/battle-for-hearts-and-minds).

findings.title: Where occupation systems produced tedium: per-unit whack-a-mole and per-state micromanagement; where they produced choice: few, consequential, portfolio-level decisions
findings.detail: The failure catalogue is consistent across the genre. Vic2/HoI3-era rebel systems spawned literal rebel stacks that the player mechanically deleted forever — pure whack-a-mole, no decision content. HoI4 pre-1.9 suppression was a solved arithmetic problem (assign N cavalry, done). Early La Resistance required clicking occupation laws state-by-state across dozens of states — Paradox later added default-law templates precisely because the per-state version was tedious even to its designers. Conversely, the systems remembered fondly are low-frequency, high-stakes: choosing an occupation LAW (a policy posture over a whole zone), deciding whether to invest in a collaboration government, Fire in the Lake's agonizing choice of which two or three provinces to pacify this turn out of twenty that need it. The lesson for your game: aggregate occupation into a handful of zones (occupied North Korea is ONE zone, maybe two), give each zone one policy choice plus a garrison slider, and let events — an uprising, a massacre incident, a defecting official — be the high-frequency texture instead of clicks.
findings.evidence: Paradox dev diary follow-ups and community threads on occupation-law micromanagement (https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/hoi4-dev-diary-resistance-and-compliance.1240349/); long-standing genre criticism of Vic2/HoI3 rebel-stack whack-a-mole (Paradox forums/community consensus); Fire in the Lake's capped Pacification as scarce-choice design (GMT rules).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Occupation Zones with two tracks (Control, Alignment) and one policy posture each
mechanics_recommendations.why: Delivers the 'hold it but don't own it' split (COIN lesson) without HoI4's per-state tedium. A zone is the decision unit — occupied North Korea is one zone — so the player makes a few consequential choices, not fifty clicks.
mechanics_recommendations.how: State: OccupationZone { provinces: Vec<ProvinceId>, occupier: CountryTag, claimant: Option<CountryTag>, control: 0..100, alignment: -100..100, policy: OccupationPolicy }. Policies as data (RON tuning): MilitaryGovernment (fast control, alignment decays, high garrison need, tension +), HandToLocalClaimant e.g. ROK administration (alignment toward claimant grows, cheaper garrison, but claimant's own legitimacy modifies it — Rhee's police in the North should cause incidents), InternationalTrusteeship (slow, low tension, requires UN-bloc standing), ExploitationRegime (immediate resource extraction, alignment collapses). Monthly system on SimClock::new_month: control += f(garrison_ratio, terrain, insurgency); alignment += g(policy, war_ongoing, sponsor_pressure, incidents). All rates in a tuning module, RNG via rng.fork(b"occupation").

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Garrison demand drawn from the real army pool
mechanics_recommendations.why: The cost of occupation must be the front line you can't reinforce (Vietnam '65 / HoI4 equipment drain — the only occupation cost players actually feel). Holding the Yalu vs. pacifying the interior becomes a genuine force-allocation dilemma with zero extra UI.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Each zone computes garrison_required = population * base_rate * (1 + insurgency_level) * policy_multiplier. Divisions assigned to garrison duty (an order state on existing units, or an abstract garrison allocation slider per zone) are unavailable for combat and take slow attrition scaled by insurgency. Shortfall => control decays, sabotage events fire, insurgency grows. This reuses the existing military layer; no parallel garrison-template subsystem.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Settlement generator at armistice: peace terms as a priced menu, with legitimacy as the output
mechanics_recommendations.why: This is the direct answer to 'no way to end the war on terms.' Every alt-history end state (status quo ante, new line, reunification, trusteeship, puppet, annexation) is a menu entry with a price paid in different currencies — and the price of skipping settlement is permanent. Kills the 'win the war get everything' button because the expensive terms are denominated in non-fungible currencies (tension, alliance cohesion, third-party acquiescence), not just war score.
mechanics_recommendations.how: When both sides are armistice-willing (existing trigger), open a Settlement instead of freezing the map. Terms: RestoreStatusQuoAnte (cheap, tension release, small standing gain), NewLine(uti possidetis or negotiated DMZ) (priced by deviation from prewar line), PuppetGovernment, Trusteeship(bloc), PlebisciteUnification (requires high alignment already earned during occupation), Annexation (astronomical: requires enemy total collapse AND great-power acquiescence). Each term has acceptance_cost(enemy) from war exhaustion/army state, and acquiescence_cost(third parties) from their stake — PRC will not acquiesce to a US-aligned unified Korea in 1950 at any normal price; that term should require either their prior defeat/exhaustion or trigger their intervention. Output: settlement_legitimacy: 0..100 stamped on the transferred territory; it sets post-war baseline resistance, sanctions pressure, and how fast the territory becomes 'owned' (cores, in HoI4 terms). No settlement => war formally unresolved: occupied zones never convert, insurgency sponsor stays active, tension floor rises.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: World Order Strain ledger (the Cold War infamy)
mechanics_recommendations.why: Vic2's key insight: internal costs are payable, external costs deter. Illegitimate territorial change must be priced in other actors' behavior — and in this game's own loss-currency, escalation. This is what makes wholesale annexation possible-but-nearly-never-worth-it rather than forbidden.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Country-level strain: u32, accrued by conquest without recognized settlement, annexation terms, exploitation policies, atrocity events; decayed slowly by recognized settlements and time. Thresholds gate AI behavior: > T1 rival aid to your insurgencies doubles, > T2 neutrals drift toward the opposing bloc and embargo, > T3 defensive coalitions form and your own alliance cohesion pays (allies distance themselves — Britain's 1950 panic over MacArthur going north is the template). Strain also feeds the existing tension number so conquest literally purchases nuclear-brinkmanship risk. Reuses the espionage system: rival covert ops targeting your occupied zones get a discount scaled by your strain.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Insurgency with an external sponsor tap
mechanics_recommendations.why: Without a sponsor/sanctuary, resistance decays into a static attrition tax the player routes around (late-game HoI4). With one, occupation stays live as long as the rivalry does, and 'cut sponsorship' becomes a negotiable settlement clause — welding occupation to the diplomacy and intel pillars.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Per-zone insurgency_level fed by: (100 - alignment), sponsor_investment (a covert-ops budget line any adjacent-or-bloc rival can fund via the existing espionage system), and border_porosity (adjacent hostile territory = sanctuary; occupied NK bordering PRC is maximally porous). Suppressed by garrison ratio and counterintel. Effects at thresholds: supply attrition, sabotage events, and at high levels province flips to partisan control requiring actual military response — resistance must occasionally threaten something real, not just tax income. Sponsor cutoff (via settlement or their own strain) puts insurgency into slow decay.

pitfalls: Per-province or per-state micromanagement: early La Resistance made players click occupation laws across dozens of states and Paradox had to patch in defaults. Keep the decision unit at the occupation-zone level (a war produces 1-3 zones), never per-province, or the system reads as chores at HoI4 scale (4,594 provinces).

Resistance as a pure attrition tax that never threatens anything: if insurgency only trims income/supply, players price it in and ignore it (late-game HoI4). It must occasionally escalate to events that demand a decision — an uprising that flips provinces, an incident that spikes tension, a sponsor escalation — or it is a rounding error with UI.

A dominant occupation policy: HoI4's long-term compliance law is nearly always correct, collapsing the choice. Policies must trade across DIFFERENT scarce currencies (garrison manpower vs money vs tension vs time vs alliance cohesion) so the right answer depends on the strategic situation, not a spreadsheet.

Pricing annexation only in fungible resources: a rich late-game player just pays any money/manpower cost. The prohibitive part of the annexation price must be non-fungible — third-party acquiescence, alliance cohesion, escalation risk, permanent insurgency — costs that cannot be out-produced.

Rebel-stack whack-a-mole (Vic2/HoI3): never spawn generic rebel armies the player mechanically deletes. Insurgency should live as zone state and events, materializing as military targets only at genuine crisis thresholds.

Frozen forever after the war: the current 'occupier keeps holding everything' end state is worse than either settlement or ongoing insurgency — an unresolved war must remain visibly unresolved (no cores, sponsor active, strain accruing), so the map itself nags the player toward a settlement.
analysts.korea_test: The moment the USA holds all of North Korea at the Yalu, the game should present a fork, not a freeze. (1) OPTIONS ON THE TABLE: Restore status quo ante (armistice at the 38th) — nearly free, releases tension, small credibility gain with allies, PRC accepts readily; this is the historically 'sane' out and should feel like a real win, not a concession. New DMZ at the current or a negotiated line (e.g. the Pyongyang–Wonsan narrow neck) — priced by deviation from the prewar line; PRC acceptance scales with their exhaustion and whether their border is buffered. Trusteeship/UN administration of the North — moderate cost, low tension, requires UN-bloc standing, produces a neutralized zone and defers the final status (this is the alt-history UNCURK path). ROK-led reunification — the big prize, and it must be expensive in the right currency: PRC acquiescence is nearly unpurchasable in 1950-51 unless China is itself defeated or exhausted, so choosing this term while the PLA is intact on the Yalu means the war continues — the cost of maximal terms is more war, which is exactly the historical mechanism (crossing the 38th bought Chinese intervention). US annexation of Korea — should exist on the menu and be strategically absurd: massive World Order Strain, allied cohesion collapse (Britain/France distance, UN mandate evaporates), permanent Soviet/PRC-sponsored insurgency, tension pinned near the brinkmanship red zone. (2) MEANWHILE, HOLDING COSTS RUN: occupied North Korea is one OccupationZone; the USA picks a posture — hand administration to Rhee's ROK (cheap garrison, but ROK legitimacy in the North is poor: alignment grows slowly and police-terror incident events spike insurgency and strain) or US military government (better control, worse optics, more tension, and it visibly delays any 'Korean' settlement). Garrison demand for ~9 million occupied people with an active PRC sanctuary next door should pin several divisions in the interior — divisions the Yalu front desperately wants, so the player feels the line thinning as the insurgency taxes the rear. (3) THE WORLD REACTS: USSR/PRC fund the northern insurgency through the espionage system (porous Yalu border = maximum sponsor tap); every month without a settlement accrues strain and holds tension at a floor; allies pressure for settlement (cohesion drains while war aims exceed the UN mandate). The dominant strategy landscape should look like: status quo ante is comfortable, a modest new line is a solid bargained win, trusteeship is the clever diplomatic play, reunification is achievable only by out-enduring China at real risk of the escalation spiral, and annexation is a trap the game permits you to walk into. If the player takes reunification and pays for it, they own a unified Korea with a decade of insurgency, a permanent garrison bill, and a Cold War running ten degrees hotter — a genuinely interesting alt-history, not a free prize."

findings.title: The real postwar menu had five dispositions — and wholesale annexation was effectively not on it
findings.detail: Between 1945 and 1990 the actual dispositions of occupied territory were: (1) RESTORE sovereignty with reform and an alliance (Japan, West Germany after 1949, South Korea after 1948); (2) SATELLITE — keep formal statehood but capture the government (Eastern Europe 1945-48, North Korea, East Germany); (3) NEUTRALIZE — withdraw in exchange for guaranteed non-alignment (Austria 1955, Finland de facto); (4) DIVIDE — freeze the line of control into two states when the powers cannot agree (Germany 1949, Korea 1948, Vietnam 1954); and (5) ANNEX, which in the UN era essentially vanished for whole states. The only wholesale annexations (Baltics, Königsberg, Kuriles, western Ukraine/Belarus) were 1940-45 faits accomplis, and even those were contested: the US maintained formal non-recognition of the Baltic annexations for fifty years, kept their legations accredited, and the annexations poisoned Soviet legitimacy permanently. Border adjustments (Oder-Neisse, Karelia) happened, but no victor after 1945 simply absorbed a defeated UN-member-scale state and had it recognized. This is the strongest historical warrant for the design requirement: annexation should not be a priced option so much as a permanently unrecognized status.
findings.evidence: US Welles Declaration non-recognition policy toward the Baltic annexations (1940-1991); Potsdam Agreement territorial provisions 1945; contrast with the recognized division outcomes of Germany (Basic Law May 1949 / GDR Oct 1949) and Korea (ROK Aug 1948 / DPRK Sep 1948).

findings.title: Satellitization took 2-4 years of staged 'salami tactics' even with total military dominance
findings.detail: Hungary is the clean timeline: the Smallholders Party won 57% of a genuinely free election in November 1945 with the Red Army occupying the country; Rákosi then proceeded in slices — control of the Interior Ministry and secret police (ÁVO) first, the fabricated 'conspiracy' and arrest of Smallholder secretary-general Béla Kovács (February 1947, by Soviet troops directly), the rigged August 1947 election, forced socialist-party merger June 1948, and a one-party state by 1949. Czechoslovakia took until the February 1948 Prague coup despite Communists having won 38% legitimately in 1946; Poland needed a rigged referendum (June 1946) and rigged election (January 1947) plus a civil war against the anti-communist underground. The lesson for design: converting occupation into a durable satellite is a multi-year political project with named intermediate steps (security ministry, purge, rigged vote, party merger), each of which was visible to the world and cost the occupier diplomatically — the 1947-48 consolidation is precisely what crystallized the Cold War (Truman Doctrine March 1947, Marshall Plan rejection July 1947).
findings.evidence: Rákosi's own coinage 'salami tactics'; Hungarian election of Nov 4 1945 and Kovács arrest Feb 25 1947; Czechoslovak coup Feb 1948; Anne Applebaum, Iron Curtain: The Crushing of Eastern Europe 1944-1956.

findings.title: Austria vs Germany: neutralization is a purchasable end-state, and division is the default when the price isn't paid
findings.detail: Austria and Germany started in the identical legal position — four-power zonal occupation from 1945 — and diverged entirely on whether a neutrality bargain closed. Germany froze: currency reform June 1948 triggered the Berlin Blockade, two states by October 1949, and no peace treaty until the Two Plus Four Treaty of 1990; the wartime occupation never got a settlement, it just hardened. Austria closed the deal: after Stalin's death, Khrushchev's leadership made permanent neutrality the condition, and the State Treaty of May 15, 1955 withdrew all four occupation armies in exchange for constitutional neutrality (declared October 26, 1955) plus a literal buyout — Austria paid the USSR $150 million out of current production plus oil deliveries for the return of 'German assets.' Ten years of occupation, ended by a side-payment and an alignment concession. For the game this is the template for the third end-state between 'my side wins the territory' and 'frozen partition': a neutralization offer that the rival bloc can accept, costing the winner the territory's alliance value and some treasure, in exchange for full withdrawal and a big tension release.
findings.evidence: Austrian State Treaty, May 15 1955 (US State Dept Office of the Historian; Britannica; countrystudies.us on the $150M payment); Berlin Blockade Jun 1948-May 1949; Two Plus Four Treaty Sep 1990.

findings.title: Restore-with-reform (Japan) was the highest-payoff disposition, but it took seven years and billions in occupier-paid upkeep
findings.detail: The US occupied Japan from September 1945 to April 28, 1952 (San Francisco Treaty signed September 1951), ran land reform, a new constitution (1947), purges and then de-purges, and pivoted in the 1947-48 'reverse course' from punishment to rebuilding an anti-communist ally. The occupier paid for it: GARIOA/EROA aid ran over $4.5 billion nominal across occupied areas — Japan received about $1.7B (rising from $92.6M in 1946 to $351.4M in 1948), Germany $1.4B in grants plus $800M in loans — on top of garrison costs. The payoff was the best in the whole period: a restored sovereign that voluntarily signed a basing/security treaty the same day as the peace treaty, giving the US its Pacific anchor without occupation costs or resistance. Germany's western zones followed the same arc (Marshall Plan 1948, semi-sovereignty 1949, full NATO accession and end of the Occupation Statute May 1955). Design translation: 'restore' should be slow (5-7 game years), expensive in treasury upkeep, but convert occupation into a willing ally with bases — the compounding-return option.
findings.evidence: CRS Report RL33331, 'U.S. Occupation Assistance: Iraq, Germany and Japan Compared'; GARIOA figures (Wikipedia/Statista per-year Japan payments); San Francisco Peace Treaty and US-Japan Security Treaty, both Sep 8 1951.

findings.title: US planning for occupied North Korea in Oct-Nov 1950 was UN-wrapped, election-based, and hedged against Chinese intervention — not annexation, and not even automatic ROK extension
findings.detail: This is the exact historical instance of the player's situation. NSC 81/1 (approved September 11, 1950) authorized ground operations north of the 38th parallel only if neither Soviet nor Chinese forces had entered, and directed that as a matter of policy only ROK forces should operate in the provinces bordering the Yalu — a constraint MacArthur discarded, with known results. The UN General Assembly resolution of October 7, 1950 created UNCURK (UN Commission for the Unification and Rehabilitation of Korea) and framed the end-state as UN-supervised elections for 'a unified, independent and democratic government,' with non-Korean UN forces to withdraw once stability was ensured. Crucially, Washington and the UN refused to recognize Syngman Rhee's claim that ROK sovereignty automatically extended north — occupied North Korea was to be under UN military government pending elections, and NSC 81/1 even directed diplomacy to have UNCURK study the NEUTRALIZATION of a unified Korea to reassure Moscow and Beijing. None of it happened because the PRC intervened in late October; the elections were never held and UNCURK lingered until 1973. The maximalist option on the table in the best case was 'UN-legitimated reunification under supervised elections, possibly neutralized' — with the occupier's hands deliberately tied to keep the great-power war away.
findings.evidence: NSC 81/1, FRUS 1950 vol. VII (history.state.gov docs 505, 531, 761); UN General Assembly Resolution 376(V), Oct 7 1950; James Matray, 'NSC-81/1 and the Evolution of U.S. War Aims in Korea June-October 1950.'

findings.title: Insurgency against consolidation ran 8-12 years and was only suppressed with mass deportation, or defeated with reform — never ignored for free
findings.detail: Soviet consolidation of the Baltics and western Ukraine faced full guerrilla wars into the mid-1950s: in Lithuania alone roughly 22,000 partisans and (by varying counts) tens of thousands of Soviet MVD/NKVD/army personnel died 1944-1953, alongside ~60,000 Lithuanian deportation deaths; against the UPA in Ukraine, Feb 1944-May 1946 alone saw ~111,000 insurgents killed, 250,000 arrested, 203,000 deported, with Operation Zakhid (October 21, 1947) deporting tens of thousands more in a single sweep. The insurgencies broke only after Stalin's death enabled the 1953 amnesties — i.e., a political event, not a purely military one, ended them. The counter-example is the Huk rebellion in the Philippines (1946-1954), defeated cheaply by Magsaysay's combination of clean 1951 elections, land-grant resettlement (EDCOR), and small-unit operations — legitimacy as counterinsurgency. Either way the finding is the same: holding territory whose disposition the population rejects imposed a decade-scale garrison and atrocity bill (Soviet path) or a serious reform/legitimacy investment (Philippine path); no occupier got quiet consolidation as the default.
findings.evidence: GlobalSecurity.org, 'Lithuanian Anti-Soviet Resistance 1944-1953' and 'Ukraine - Anti-Soviet Partisans'; Operation Zakhid Oct 1947; Lawrence Greenberg / US Army CMH studies of the Hukbalahap campaign and Magsaysay's EDCOR program.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: War-termination settlement packages priced in recognition, not just territory
mechanics_recommendations.why: Historically every disposition beyond status-quo restoration required third parties (the rival superpower, the UN) to bless it — Austria needed a Soviet signature, Korean reunification needed a UN mandate, and unblessed outcomes (GDR, annexed Baltics) carried permanent non-recognition. A peace screen that only bargains with the defeated enemy misses that great-power recognition is the real currency.
mechanics_recommendations.how: At armistice-willingness, open a settlement negotiation with a menu of disposition clauses per occupied region: Restore (status quo ante), Adjust Line (new border at/near line of control), Neutralize (independent, forced non-aligned, both blocs withdraw), Trusteeship/Supervised Elections (UN-flagged transition state), Satellite (puppet government of your ideology), or Unilateral Hold (no agreement — occupation continues, war formally ends or freezes). Each clause has an acceptance cost computed from: enemy's remaining war capacity, rival-bloc tension, and world-opinion stock. Settlements the rival bloc signs grant 'recognized' status (tension release, trade normal, occupation ends); settlements imposed without signature leave the territory in Unrecognized status — a persistent flag, not a one-time fee — carrying a tension floor, trade/diplo penalties, and external support for resistance until a later recognition event (leadership change on the rival side, à la Stalin's death 1953, is the natural unlock).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Occupation as ongoing state: authority, upkeep, and a consolidation clock
mechanics_recommendations.why: Real occupations cost the occupier continuously — GARIOA-scale civilian aid ($100-350M/year per country in 1940s dollars), garrison manpower, and years of time (Japan 7, Austria 10, satellite consolidation 3-4, insurgency suppression 8-12). The current 'frozen map of occupier tags' gives victory with zero carrying cost, which is exactly the free-annexation failure the design forbids.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Give each occupied region an Occupation struct: authority (0-100, grows monthly with garrison strength and civil spending, shrinks with resistance and war), a monthly upkeep drain (civil administration + relief, scaling with population and destruction), and a garrison requirement (divisions that cannot be used elsewhere without authority decay). Disposition clauses are gated on authority thresholds and elapsed time: Satellite requires ~3 years of staged steps, Restore/Elections ~2 years plus high authority, Neutralize is available immediately if the rival signs. Withdrawal or negotiated settlement zeroes the drain; holding indefinitely never does. Tick this in the Politics stage on SimClock::new_month, tuning values in a marked tuning module per project convention.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Legitimacy pathway: UN mandate and supervised elections as the 'good' reunification route
mechanics_recommendations.why: The October 7, 1950 UN resolution and UNCURK show the historically available maximal outcome for the player's exact position: reunification was possible but only through a UN-wrapped election process, with occupier troops restricted and eventual withdrawal promised — and NSC 81/1 even contemplated neutralizing the result. This gives the game its alt-history 'reunified Korea' end-state without an annexation button.
mechanics_recommendations.how: If the war carries a UN/coalition mandate (track this on the war object), the victor may initiate a Supervised Transition: a 18-30 month timer during which elections are organized. Requirements: authority above a threshold, non-defeated-nationality garrisons kept below a cap near rival-bloc borders (violating the cap spikes intervention risk — the MacArthur rule), and continued upkeep spending. Outcome on completion: a new unified state aligned to the occupier (influence-warfare pillar sets HOW aligned — election result = f(authority, ideology influence, war devastation, rival covert ops)), with full recognition and a large tension release. Rival covert ops and border pressure can sabotage the timer, making the intelligence pillar matter. Offering to also Neutralize the resulting state massively raises rival acceptance — the Austria lever applied to Korea.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Resistance and counter-consolidation with politically-legible tools
mechanics_recommendations.why: Baltic/Ukrainian resistance cost the USSR a decade, six-figure deportations, and world-standing; the Huks were beaten by reform and clean elections. Resistance should punish illegitimate dispositions specifically, and the occupier's response should be a real choice between the Soviet path (fast, brutal, world-opinion catastrophe) and the Magsaysay path (slow, expensive, clean).
mechanics_recommendations.how: Resistance per occupied region = f(disposition legitimacy, ideology distance, rival covert support, terrain). It drains authority, kills garrison manpower monthly, and can flare into open revolt. Occupier responses as policies: Reform (high upkeep, slow resistance decay, world-opinion neutral), Repression (raises short-term authority, resistance decays but world-opinion and tension pay), Mass Deportation (atrocity action: near-terminal resistance suppression, severe permanent world-opinion and ideology-pillar penalties, escalation risk). Rival-bloc leadership-change events (modeled on March 1953) offer amnesty windows that let long insurgencies actually end. Unrecognized territories get a standing rival-funded resistance floor that recognized ones do not — this is what makes recognition mechanically real.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: The salami track: satellitization as a staged multi-year project
mechanics_recommendations.why: Making a puppet was never a checkbox; it was a visible sequence (security ministry, purges, rigged election, party merger) over 2-4 years, each step ratcheting Cold War tension — the 1947-48 consolidations CREATED the Truman Doctrine and the blocs. Staging it gives the ideology and intel pillars something to do during peace and lets rivals interfere mid-process.
mechanics_recommendations.how: The Satellite disposition spawns a project with 4-5 ordered stages (install coalition government → seize interior ministry → purge opposition → managed election → one-party merger), each taking 4-8 months, costing intel-network capacity and money, raising world tension on completion, and vulnerable to rival covert ops (a failed stage can flip to the Czechoslovak-in-reverse: a coup against you, or an uprising). Completing all stages yields a recognized-by-your-bloc puppet with your ideology; abandoning midway leaves an unstable client. Reuse the espionage v1 network/ops machinery already in the codebase as the interference surface.

pitfalls: Pricing annexation instead of delegitimizing it. If wholesale annexation is merely expensive, players will pay the number and the design requirement fails. History's actual mechanism was permanent non-recognition — a status that never stops costing (tension floor, trade exclusion, funded resistance, no alliance value from the territory) until an explicit later recognition event. Model it as a persistent flag with ongoing consequences, not a one-time cost, and make genuine whole-state annexation of the Korea/Germany class simply not a clause the settlement screen offers (border adjustments, yes; absorbing a state, no).

Instant consolidation. Every historical disposition took years — 3-4 to satellite Hungary with the Red Army already there, 7 to restore Japan, 10 to settle Austria, 8-12 to crush the Forest Brothers. If a disposition resolves the moment the treaty is signed, the occupation/resistance/consolidation layer never runs and the mid-game disappears. Every disposition except Restore-status-quo needs a clock with things happening on it.

Negotiating only with the defeated. Austria's treaty needed Moscow's signature, Korea's reunification needed a UN mandate, Germany froze precisely because the four powers could not agree. A war-termination system whose acceptance check involves only the beaten enemy will produce ahistorical clean victories; the rival superpower must be a party (or a refuser whose refusal creates the Unrecognized/frozen-conflict outcome).

Making resistance generic attrition. If occupation resistance is just a hitpoint drain, the Soviet-vs-Magsaysay strategic choice — brutality that trades world opinion for speed versus reform that trades treasure for legitimacy — vanishes, and with it the tie-ins to the ideology and escalation pillars. Resistance responses need to be named policies with distinct pillar-visible costs, and political events (enemy leadership change, amnesties) need to be able to end insurgencies, not just military suppression.
analysts.korea_test: The player holds all of North Korea at the Yalu with PRC forces across the river — exactly the position of late October 1950 before Chinese intervention, so history supplies the option menu directly. OPTIONS THAT SHOULD EXIST: (1) Restore status quo ante (withdraw to the 38th) — cheapest: immediate armistice acceptance, large tension release with both PRC and USSR, war-weariness relief, but zero territorial gain and a domestic-politics cost for 'giving back' a won war. (2) Adjust the line — a new border at the Pyongyang-Wonsan 'narrow waist' (an actual contemplated fallback) or wherever the front sits: moderate rival acceptance if the line leaves a DPRK rump buffer on the Yalu; creates the alt-history DMZ. (3) Supervised Transition (the UNCURK path) — because this war carries a UN mandate, the player may run the 18-30 month elections track toward a reunified, US-aligned Korea; requirements are the historical constraints turned into rules: keep US/UN (non-ROK) divisions below a cap in the Yalu border provinces or PRC intervention risk climbs sharply, sustain occupation upkeep (GARIOA-scale, a real monthly treasury drain), and hold authority against northern partisan resistance fed by Chinese covert support. Offering to NEUTRALIZE the unified Korea (no US bases, non-aligned — NSC 81/1's own idea, the Austria model) sharply raises Soviet/PRC acceptance and may get the settlement signed and recognized; refusing neutralization means Moscow and Beijing likely never sign, and even a successful election yields a unified Korea in Unrecognized status with a permanent tension floor and a live Chinese threat. (4) Satellite — install Rhee (or a client) over the whole peninsula unilaterally via the salami track: no rival signature, so Unrecognized status, standing PRC-funded insurgency in the northern provinces, a large permanent garrison pinned on the Yalu, and the rival bloc's armistice willingness for THIS settlement never materializes — the war can freeze but not close. (5) Wholesale annexation (Korea becomes US territory) should not be on the menu at all — no 1945-90 precedent, and it is the design's forbidden free-win. WHAT THE AI/WORLD DOES: the PRC treats non-Korean troops massed on the Yalu as an intervention trigger (a rising monthly risk roll, exactly the NSC 81/1 fear MacArthur ignored — the player who garrisons the border with ROK units instead is playing the constraint correctly); the USSR bankrolls northern resistance and vetoes recognition of any un-neutralized reunification; world opinion rewards the UN-wrapped paths and punishes repression policies used against northern resistance; and a Soviet leadership-change event in the mid-1950s (the Stalin's-death analogue) reopens recognition and amnesty possibilities for whatever frozen or unrecognized outcome the player chose. Sources behind this application: NSC 81/1 and FRUS 1950 vol. VII (history.state.gov), UN GA Resolution 376(V) of Oct 7 1950 creating UNCURK, the Austrian State Treaty of May 15 1955 as the neutralization template, and the CRS occupation-assistance cost data (RL33331).

analysts.analyst: Paradox war-termination lens (EU4 / CK3 / Victoria 3 / Stellaris): war goals, war score, infamy, truces, diplomatic plays

findings.title: Declaring the objective before (or at) the start of the war is the single strongest limited-war technology Paradox ever built
findings.detail: Every Paradox game that produces plausibly-limited wars does it by making the war's purpose a first-class, pre-declared game object: EU4's casus belli scopes what peace options are cheap, CK3's single-wargoal wars end with exactly that goal enforced or denied (you literally cannot take more than you declared), and Victoria 3's diplomatic plays make you attach every demand to the crisis before shooting starts, priced in infamy up front. The declared aim does three jobs at once: it defines a checkable victory condition (so the war can END without anyone being annihilated), it gives the AI a legible thing to accept or refuse, and it makes overreach a visible, priced act rather than an emergent accident. CK3 is the purest proof: because the wargoal is the whole peace treaty, wars are short, ends are clean, and 'I won, now what?' never happens. The failure mode is the opposite end — EU4 lets you seize anything at warscore cost regardless of CB, which is exactly how limited wars quietly become conquest engines. For a Cold War game where the thesis is limited war, war aims should be the spine of the entire war state, not an afterthought at the peace screen.
findings.evidence: Victoria 3 Dev Diary #21 (Diplomatic Plays) — demands set during escalation, backing down concedes only the Main Demand, infamy refunded for unpressed demands: https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/victoria-3-dev-diary-21-diplomatic-plays.1495892/ ; CK3's single-wargoal war design; EU4 CB/warscore peace rules (any province seizable at warscore + AE cost).

findings.title: Infamy/AE/threat only constrains the player when it is spent through multiple channels; a single threshold cliff becomes a solved meta
findings.detail: EU4's Aggressive Expansion is per-observer, distance-scaled, and decays linearly — good bones — but its only real teeth are coalitions, which fire at a known threshold (50 AE, outraged attitude). The community solved it years ago: 'coalition juggling' — take land in sub-threshold bites, truce-lock would-be coalition members, park armies to deter joiners, wait out predictable decay. The punishment is binary (coalition or nothing), so play optimizes to 49. Stellaris's threat/containment has the same shape and same exploit. Victoria 3's infamy is better in kind — it feeds diplomatic plays against you, sway costs, and pariah status, i.e. continuous multi-channel pressure — but is undertuned for great powers, who can eat infamy freely. The design lesson is structural, not tuning: the price of taking territory must leak into several systems at once (who aligns with your rival, what your own public tolerates, what crises get started against you, what you can no longer buy diplomatically), decay slowly with memory, and never reduce to one number with one known trigger. For this game, the four pillars ARE the channels: influence standing, escalation posture, intel exposure, and economic alignment of neutrals.
findings.evidence: Community-documented coalition-juggling meta and AE criticism: https://www.fandomspot.com/eu4-handling-aggressive-expansion-coalitions/ and https://steamcommunity.com/app/236850/discussions/0/4477133359558064908/ ; Vic3 infamy design (DD#21 and subsequent balance passes weakening/strengthening infamy for great powers).

findings.title: Ticking war score — score from HOLDING the declared objective over time — is the mechanism that actually ends wars; occupation-percentage score is the mechanism that prolongs them
findings.detail: In EU4, warscore from battles and sieges makes negotiation an accounting grind (chase stacks for +2%, siege one more fort), and 100%-warscore peace pushes toward maximal extraction. But EU4's ticking warscore — you passively gain score each month you hold the CB's named objective — is quietly the best idea in the system: it rewards achieving what you declared, punishes fighting past it, and gives the losing side a reason to settle before the ledger worsens. Stellaris shows the complementary piece: status quo peace draws the border at the line of control, but ONLY claimed systems transfer — unclaimed occupation reverts. That pair (time-pressure from holding your declared aim + reversion of everything you didn't legitimize) is precisely an armistice-negotiation model. The failure to avoid: any settlement leverage derived from cumulative destruction (battles won, provinces sieged) turns a Cold War limited conflict into an incentive to widen it. Leverage should come from position-versus-aims, time, and each side's remaining political will — nothing else.
findings.evidence: EU4 ticking warscore mechanics (EU4 wiki, warscore/peace treaties); Stellaris status quo = claimed-and-occupied systems transfer, unclaimed occupation reverts: https://stellaris.paradoxwikis.com/Console:Warfare and https://stellaris.fandom.com/wiki/Warfare ; longstanding warscore-micro criticism in EU4 community discussions: https://steamcommunity.com/app/236850/discussions/0/366298942096734632/

findings.title: War exhaustion must be an acceptance modifier, not a hard timer — Stellaris's forced status quo is the cautionary tale
findings.detail: Stellaris ends wars by force: 24 months after you hit 100% war exhaustion the enemy can impose status quo, full stop. Players hate it enough that 'No Forced Peace' mods are perennial and forum threads document wars locked in absurd states by the timer; the mechanic reads as arbitrary because it overrides a player who is materially winning. EU4's 'Call for Peace' and war exhaustion do the same job better: mounting costs (stability hits, unrest, manpower) and acceptance-score pressure that make continuing painful but never impossible. For a Cold War game this maps onto the historically correct resource: domestic political will. Korea and Vietnam were not lost at the front; they were lost at home. Political will as a per-belligerent pool — drained by casualties, duration, escalation scares, and refusing reasonable settlement offers; restored by achieving declared aims — gives you exhaustion that is diegetic, asymmetric (democracies drain faster, but autocracies crack harder), and never confiscates agency: a player may always keep fighting, at compounding domestic cost.
findings.evidence: Stellaris forced-status-quo frustration: https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/locked-at-100-war-exhaustion-without-possibility-for-status-quo.1505871/ and the No-Forced-Peace mod family; EU4 Call for Peace / war exhaustion as soft pressure; historical: Korean War armistice politics 1951-53 (two years of fighting during negotiations over acceptance terms, not territory).

findings.title: Victoria 3's diplomatic play is the right skeleton for a game where wars are rare: war is the failure tail of a crisis process, and backing down is a first-class outcome
findings.detail: Vic3 reframed war initiation as a multi-phase crisis: opening moves, maneuvering (sway third parties with promised demands, add demands — each pausing escalation so the other side can react), then countdown-to-war where the only remaining move is backing down. Most plays never become wars; when they do, the sides, stakes, and third-party commitments were all fixed in advance. Only the Main Demand is conceded by a back-down — pressing multiple demands requires actually fighting — which elegantly makes big revisions expensive and small ones negotiable. This is the Cold War in mechanical form: Berlin blockades and missile crises are diplomatic plays, and the game's escalation pillar already wants exactly this ladder. The steal for war TERMINATION specifically: symmetry. The same crisis machinery should run in reverse at the end of a war — a settlement is a play where the demands are the standing war aims, sweeteners can be added from outside the theater (recognition, UN seats, trade), and 'backing down' from an aim is a priced, face-losing but legitimate move, not a defeat screen.
findings.evidence: Victoria 3 Dev Diary #21 — phase structure, escalation pauses on sways/demands, back-down concedes Main Demand only, infamy refund for unpressed demands: https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/victoria-3-dev-diary-21-diplomatic-plays.1495892/

findings.title: Truces and treaty objects are what make outcomes STICK; the current 'occupation frozen forever' is a missing treaty layer, not a missing conquest layer
findings.detail: Paradox games make peace durable with two devices: truce timers (re-declaration within the truce carries severe stability/infamy penalties — EU4's ~5-15 year truces, Stellaris's 10-year forced open borders and truces) and, in Vic3, treaties as persistent objects with articles and violation consequences. The player's Korea situation is exactly what happens when a war ends without producing a treaty object: the map remembers who stands where, but the world remembers nothing — no obligations, no recognized borders, no cost to the anomaly. The steal: every war termination must instantiate a Settlement entity — parties, territorial articles (cessions, DMZ strips, plebiscite schedules, trusteeships, puppet creations), truce duration, and guarantor signatures — that other systems can read. Recognition is the Cold War-specific extension no Paradox game does well: a cession signed only by the beaten party but not recognized by the rival bloc (East Germany, the DPRK itself, PRC-on-Taiwan) should be a treaty in a degraded state, generating friction until recognized. That single concept generates divided-Germany/divided-Korea texture for free.
findings.evidence: EU4 truce and truce-breaking penalties (EU4 wiki); Stellaris post-surrender 10-year open borders + truce: https://stellaris.paradoxwikis.com/Console:Warfare ; Victoria 3's 1.5 'Colossus of the South' treaty rework toward persistent treaty objects; historical: the Korean Armistice Agreement is itself a 70-year-old armistice-without-peace-treaty — the game state the player is missing.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Declared War Aims as the spine of every war (with priced mid-war revision)
mechanics_recommendations.why: Scopes the war before/as it starts, gives the AI a legible acceptance target, makes the settlement screen buildable (aims are the menu), and turns overreach — the exact Korea moment of crossing the 38th — into an explicit, priced player decision instead of an emergent accident. This is the CK3/Vic3 lesson: wars end cleanly because their purpose is a game object.
mechanics_recommendations.how: State: each war holds `Vec<WarAim { owner: CountryTag, kind: AimKind, added: SimDate, legitimacy: i32 }>` where AimKind is a small closed enum — StatusQuoAnte, NewLine(Vec<ProvinceId>), RegimeChange(CountryTag), UnifyUnder(CountryTag), Puppet(CountryTag), DMZ(Vec<ProvinceId>), Trusteeship(region) — data-driven prices in a tuning file. A war gets a default aim at declaration (defender always holds StatusQuoAnte free). Adding or upgrading an aim mid-war is a command with costs scaled by aim severity: world tension spike, political-will hit at home if it extends the war, and a large intervention-weight bonus for the enemy's patrons (crossing the 38th mechanically CAUSES the PRC entry the game already models). Aims are visible to all parties — no hidden win conditions.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Settlement Table replacing the automatic armistice: acceptance-scored negotiated peace
mechanics_recommendations.why: The current auto-armistice hardcodes exactly one outcome (line of control, no terms). A negotiation screen with a transparent acceptance ledger produces every alt-history end state the player wants — reunification either way, status quo ante, new DMZ, puppets, trusteeships — while making each one cost what it should. EU4's acceptance-number-with-visible-reasons is the model; Stellaris's hidden/forced outcomes are the anti-model.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Either side may propose a settlement (a bundle of articles drawn from the standing aims plus sweeteners: recognition, aid, off-theater concessions). Acceptance per opposing belligerent = f(military position vs each article: fully-occupied articles cheap, articles beyond the line of control very expensive; both sides' political-will pools; patron pressure; time since front moved; escalation fear). Deterministic integer math, every term shown as a ledger row. Accepted settlement instantiates a `Treaty` entity executing territorial transfers, puppet/DMZ/trusteeship creation, a truce timer, and per-signatory recognition flags; scheduled articles (plebiscite in N months) become sim events. Ticking pressure: when the front is static AND one side's aims are fully occupied, a monthly 'call for settlement' drains political will from whoever refuses terms the acceptance math scores as reasonable — this is EU4's ticking warscore + Call for Peace fused, and it is what finally forces the table.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Occupation-vs-annexation split: unsettled occupation is expensive and reverts; annexation requires treaty or costs infamy across all four pillars
mechanics_recommendations.why: This is the anti-'transfer everything to me' button. Stellaris's rule that unclaimed occupation reverts at status quo is the core steal: holding territory and owning it are different legal states. The Cold War extension is recognition — annexation the world refuses to recognize should be a permanent running sore, which is both historically right and mechanically the multi-channel infamy spend that EU4's single coalition-cliff lacks.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Occupied provinces get an `Occupation { occupier, since, resistance: u8 }` component while the war is live or unsettled. Costs while occupying: garrison requirement (divisions pinned, unavailable to the front), monthly political-will drain scaled by resistance, world-tension floor, and rival-bloc resistance sponsorship hooks (feeds the existing espionage pillar — networks fund partisans). At settlement, provinces not covered by a treaty article revert to prewar owner over a withdrawal timer. Unilateral annexation exists as a command but prices through every pillar: large infamy (influence standing of neutrals drifts toward the rival bloc, ~Vic3 infamy but spent continuously), non-recognition state (trade and diplomacy penalties with every non-recognizer, no legitimacy income from the territory), permanent insurgency eligibility, and escalation-acceptance bonus for the rival (they run bigger risks against a pariah). No threshold cliff — every point of infamy buys the other side something, and decay has memory (halts while any non-recognized annexation stands).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Political Will as the war-exhaustion resource (soft clock, never a hard timer)
mechanics_recommendations.why: Stellaris proves hard forced-peace timers are hated; EU4 proves soft acceptance pressure works. Political will is the historically correct Cold War exhaustion currency — limited wars are lost at home — and it doubles as the payment medium for aim inflation, refusing settlements, and occupation, unifying the whole termination system around one legible pool.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Per-belligerent `PoliticalWill(i32)` pool, government-type-dependent cap and drain curves (democracies: fast drain from casualties and duration, recover on settlement; autocracies: slow drain, but crossing low thresholds risks internal crisis events rather than gentle pressure). Drains: monthly base while at war, casualties, escalation incidents, occupation upkeep, refusing 'reasonable' settlement offers (acceptance-math-positive offers the player declines). Gains: achieving a declared aim, successful settlements, rally events. Effects are graduated modifiers (recruitment, acceptance penalties on YOUR side of the ledger, election/legitimacy events), never a forced peace — the player who wants to fight to zero may, and eats the domestic consequences the game already knows how to model.

pitfalls: The single-threshold punishment cliff. If the cost of overreach reduces to one number with one known trigger (EU4's 50-AE coalition), players will solve it — dance at 49, truce-lock the enforcers, wait out linear decay. Costs of conquest must be continuous (every point buys the rival something), multi-channel (influence, escalation, intel, economy), and hysteretic (decay pauses while the grievance — e.g. an unrecognized annexation — still stands).

Warscore micro and the destruction treadmill. Deriving settlement leverage from cumulative battles/sieges (EU4) makes players chase stacks for percentage points and rewards WIDENING a war to afford the peace deal — the exact opposite of the limited-war thesis. Leverage must come only from position-versus-declared-aims, time, and political will; destroying more things must never be the way to buy a better border.

Hard forced peace that overrides a winning player (Stellaris's 100%-exhaustion status quo). It reads as arbitrary confiscation of agency and spawns removal mods. Exhaustion should make continuing increasingly expensive and settlement increasingly attractive — never impossible to refuse.

War aims as a straitjacket OR as a fig leaf. If aims are frozen at declaration, the fun alt-history (crossing the 38th to unify Korea) is blocked and the system fights the player; if aims can be revised freely, it is HoI4 conquest with extra steps. Mid-war revision must exist and must be the most expensive diplomatic act in the game — tension spike, political-will cost, and mechanical patron-intervention triggers.

Opaque AI acceptance. If the settlement AI is a hidden willingness flag (the current 10-months+static-front heuristic), players experience refusal as a bug, not a negotiation. Show the full acceptance ledger EU4-style — every article's cost, every modifier — so 'the PRC will never accept a unified Korea while its army stands on the Yalu' is a readable fact the player can plan against, not a mystery.

Letting the defender's default be conquest-symmetric. The defender must always hold Status Quo Ante as a free standing aim; otherwise every defensive war the AI wins becomes its own annexation problem, and white peace / restoration stops being a respected, cheap, dignified outcome — which it must be for a game where most wars should end roughly where they started.
analysts.korea_test: Reconstructing the situation in the recommended system: the US/UN entered with the defender-side free aim StatusQuoAnte (restore the 38th). Crossing the parallel was an explicit aim-upgrade command to UnifyUnder(ROK) — it cost political will and tension, and it mechanically fired the PRC intervention weight (which the game already produced). Now the player holds all of NK at the Yalu, at war with the PRC, and opens the Settlement Table. Options and prices: (1) UnifyUnder(ROK) — the article is fully occupied, so its occupation term is cheap, but PRC/USSR acceptance is catastrophically negative while the PLA is intact and their political will is high; getting to yes requires either years more war on the Yalu (draining US political will monthly, holding tension near nuclear-temptation levels — the MacArthur option to nuke acceptance into existence lives in the escalation pillar and prices accordingly) or massive off-theater sweeteners (recognize the PRC, UN seat, Taiwan-adjacent concessions) — possible, historic-plausible, and expensive, exactly as required. (2) NewLine at the narrow neck (Pyongyang-Wonsan) with a DMZ article — moderately negative acceptance that turns positive once PRC offensives fail and their will drains; produces a treaty with a DMZ province strip, truce timer, and a rump DPRK. (3) StatusQuoAnte — accepted almost immediately, tension drops, the player banks partial political-will recovery for achieving the original defensive aim; the respectable white peace. (4) Trusteeship/plebiscite article — UN trusteeship over NK with a scheduled plebiscite event in 24 months; lower infamy than unification, delayed and riskier payoff (the influence pillar decides the plebiscite). (5) Refuse to settle and just hold: every NK province carries Occupation state — garrisons pinned away from the Yalu front, USSR/PRC-sponsored resistance rising through the espionage system, monthly political-will drain, elevated world-tension floor, allied drift — and the monthly call-for-settlement ticks against the US because its aims are occupied and the front is static. (6) Unilateral annexation/ROK absorption with no treaty: available, never free — non-recognition by the entire communist bloc and most neutrals, continuous infamy spend pushing neutral alignment toward Moscow, permanent insurgency eligibility, and infamy decay frozen while the annexation stands unrecognized. The AI side runs the same math: PRC acceptance is a visible ledger (army intact +, will draining -, USSR pressure term), the USSR responds off-theater (resistance sponsorship, a Europe crisis play if tension allows), and no outcome is a button — every end state is a priced negotiation the world remembers via the Treaty object.

analysts.analyst: HoI4 war-termination analyst (peace conferences, capitulation, occupation)

findings.title: All-or-nothing capitulation makes limited war structurally impossible — the single deepest flaw
findings.detail: In HoI4 a war ends in exactly two ways: one entire side capitulates (loses enough victory points) and a peace conference fires, or the war grinds on forever. There is no conditional surrender, no negotiated line, no partial concession — a decade-old community complaint, and an entire genre of mods (HOI4+: Conditional Surrender, Make Peace Not War, Player Led Peace Conferences) exists purely to patch it. The root cause is architectural: HoI4 has no concept of war AIMS or negotiable stakes during the war; peace is a terminal minigame, not a bargaining process, so a Korean-War-shaped conflict (fight, stalemate, armistice on terms) cannot be expressed at all. UGS already has armistice-at-line-of-control, which is genuinely ahead of HoI4 here — the missing piece is pricing TERMS on top of that armistice, not replacing it with a conference.
findings.evidence: Paradox forum thread 'Capitulation: Why does defeat seem to assume unconditional surrender?' (forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/capitulation-why-does-defeat-seem-to-assume-unconditional-surrender.1140022); Steam Workshop 'HOI4+: Conditional Surrender' (steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2271920262) and 'Make Peace, Not War' (id=1133300976), both framed explicitly as fixes for dead-end total wars.

findings.title: War score as a fungible spendable currency is what produced the shopping sprees and border spaghetti
findings.detail: Pre-rework, peace conference turn order went by war participation, and score was earned chiefly by casualties TAKEN, not inflicted or ground held — 'the man who loses the most men gets the most land.' Score was one undifferentiated pot spendable on any state anywhere: points earned bleeding in Africa bought Tokyo. This is the mechanism behind every famous failure: the USA lands one division, joins the faction, and out-bids the player for half of Germany; players who conquered a country solo can't afford the states they physically occupy; the map ends as ahistorical patchwork. The design lesson is that claims must be BOUND to specific territory (occupation, declared aims, historical cores), never abstract points — a fungible victory currency plus a free-for-all spending phase mathematically guarantees ahistorical outcomes.
findings.evidence: Paradox forum 'Peace Conferences are the worse mechanic imaginable' (forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/peace-conferences-are-the-worse-mechanic-imaginable.1409021); Steam discussions on allies taking everything (steamcommunity.com/app/394360/discussions/0/3185654583887167101) and being unable to claim conquered territory (discussions/0/3368153565084560376); popularity of the Player Led Peace Conference mod as a community bypass.

findings.title: The By Blood Alone rework (1.12, Sept 2022) fixed the process but not the premise
findings.detail: The rework replaced sequential turn-order grabbing with simultaneous blind bidding turns where every action is contestable (highest bidder wins a contested state), split war contribution so it is earned where you actually fought, and added richer demand types: reparations (factories/resources), demilitarized zones, taking the enemy navy — real steps toward settlements that are not pure land transfer. What it did NOT fix: the conference still only fires at total capitulation, so limited war remains impossible; it is still a one-shot minigame after the war rather than negotiation during it; annexation is still a one-time purchase with no legitimacy cost afterward; and post-rework threads ('The New Peace System is terrible', bug reports like being unable to give territory away without taking something) show the deal outcomes still read as nonsense. Verdict: bidding/contesting and category-scoped contribution are worth stealing; the fire-at-capitulation trigger and the after-the-fact conference framing are the parts that must be avoided.
findings.evidence: By Blood Alone 'Peace Conference Roundup' dev diary (forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/developer-diary/developer-diary-peace-conference-roundup.1538768); HoI4 wiki Peace conference page (hoi4.paradoxwikis.com/Peace_conference); Steam discussion 'The New Peace System is terrible' (steamcommunity.com/app/394360/discussions/0/3392923906951996847) and post-rework bug threads (discussions/0/3392923906933998642).

findings.title: La Resistance built the right occupation-cost engine but never wired it to war termination
findings.detail: The 1.9 Resistance & Compliance system (2020) is HoI4's best half-answer to 'annexation must not be free': resistance drifts toward a target set by state development and whether the core owner still exists; garrisons are a shield that consumes manpower and equipment against sabotage; compliance grows slowly and unlocks cooperation; high resistance escalates to attrition maluses and full uprisings. Paradox explicitly framed it as putting 'a clock on world conquest runs.' But it is completely decoupled from peace: the conference prices annexation identically whether a state is 90% compliant or in open revolt, compliance never converts into recognized ownership, and once annexed the land eventually becomes normal territory. The steal for UGS: occupation politics should BE the price signal for territorial terms — what you can pacify and administer is what you can plausibly keep, and the settlement system should read that state directly.
findings.evidence: HoI4 Dev Diary — Resistance and Compliance (forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/hoi4-dev-diary-resistance-and-compliance.1240349): target-driven resistance, garrison-as-shield, compliance ladder, uprisings, and the stated design goal of curbing snowballing and clocking world conquests.

findings.title: HoI4 has no international-consequence layer for conquest — world tension is a trigger, not a cost
findings.detail: World tension in HoI4 gates AI decisions (joining factions, lend-lease) but conquest itself carries almost no downstream price: no recognition question, no sanctions, no legitimacy, no containment coalition forming against the winner, no diplomatic memory. The winner of a war faces a world that shrugs. For a WWII total-war game that is merely thin; for a Cold War game it is disqualifying, because the entire historical logic of 1950 Korea was third-party reaction — Chinese intervention triggered by approaching the Yalu, Soviet calibration, UN legitimacy, domestic war-weariness. UGS's existing 'tension number' is currently in the same trap. The consequence system for conquest is not an add-on to war termination, it is the load-bearing wall: unrecognized territorial change must generate ongoing pressure through all four pillars (tension/escalation, ideology/propaganda, insurgency via espionage, embargo via economy).
findings.evidence: HoI4 wiki world tension mechanics plus the absence of any recognition/sanction system in base game or DLC; historical grounding: Chinese intervention Oct 1950 as reaction to UN forces nearing the Yalu, and the 1953 armistice-without-peace-treaty as the canonical 'unresolved settlement' end state.

findings.title: Puppets and collaboration governments are HoI4's most Cold-War-relevant tool — victory should usually produce a client, not a color change
findings.detail: Puppeting in HoI4 costs far less war score than annexation, keeps borders historically plausible, and (with Together for Victory) sits on an autonomy ladder from integrated puppet to free ally. La Resistance's collaboration governments add the best wrinkle: political preparation DURING the war (covert ops raising collaboration) lowers the enemy surrender threshold and yields a better client afterward — the war's political endgame is shaped before the shooting stops. This is exactly the Cold War pattern (ROK, DPRK, FRG, GDR are all somebody's client) and it directly serves UGS's requirement that alt-history end states be possible but annexation costly: the cheap, recognized, stable outcome is a friendly government, and the espionage/ideology pillars become the tools that make it cheaper.
findings.evidence: HoI4 peace conference cost structure (puppet vs annex, hoi4.paradoxwikis.com/Peace_conference); Together for Victory autonomy system; La Resistance collaboration government mechanic (raise collaboration via intel ops pre-capitulation for reduced surrender limit and better puppet).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Negotiated settlement: offer/counter-offer over discrete priced terms, replacing any 'conference at capitulation'
mechanics_recommendations.why: HoI4's terminal minigame is the thing to avoid; UGS already has armistice-at-LoC, which should become the zero-term baseline settlement with everything else priced on top. Wars must be fought FOR terms, evaluable at any moment, so a stalemate at the Yalu is a negotiating position, not a dead end.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Add a WarAims/SettlementOffer structure per war: a list of terms, each targeting concrete provinces or polities — StatusQuoAnte, NewLine(province set at LoC), Dmz(province set), Plebiscite(region, date), ClientState{autonomy level}, Trusteeship{administrators}, Annex(province set), Reparations, Demilitarization. Each term has severity(term, target). AI acceptance is a deterministic monthly evaluation: acceptance = base_willingness(months_at_war, months_static_front, casualties/manpower, fraction_home_occupied, army_integrity) + patron_pressure − Σ severity_i × resistance_discount_i. Offers are commands; AI counters by dropping the highest-severity terms it cannot swallow. Surface the full acceptance math in UI (players must see WHY a term is refused and what would change it). Runs in TickSet::Politics on SimClock::new_day, RNG only via rng.fork(b"settlement").

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Occupation as a live cost meter that prices the settlement (pacification per occupied province)
mechanics_recommendations.why: La Resistance proved the occupation-cost engine works but HoI4 never connected it to peace pricing — the connection is the whole point. It makes 'annex everything' self-limiting without any hard rule, and makes holding ground a strategic investment rather than a frozen map overlay.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Per occupied province: pacification in [0,1] drifting toward a target = f(ideology distance occupier↔local population, war conduct events, garrison policy chosen from a small law set, existence of a government-in-exile, rival-bloc insurgency funding). Monthly costs while occupied and unsettled: garrison manpower + budget upkeep + tension trickle. Low pacification spawns partisan events (supply attrition, intel penalties — feeds espionage pillar as a target for both sides). In the settlement evaluator, severity of Annex/ClientState terms over a province scales inversely with its pacification and with historical-claim status (recovered cores and plebiscite-won provinces near-free; hostile un-pacified land priced beyond acceptance). Numbers live in a tuning module; province pacification is new sim state alongside the existing occupier map.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Recognition layer: settlements are signed and recognized, unilateral changes are not — and unrecognized change bleeds forever
mechanics_recommendations.why: The 'no free annexation' requirement fails if the cost is one-time — players happily pay any up-front price. HoI4's missing consequence layer must be ongoing: the deterrent to conquest is that the world never accepts it. This also natively produces the Korea outcome — an armistice WITHOUT a settlement is itself a playable, historically真 state (frozen conflict, DMZ, ongoing costs), which is exactly what 1953 was.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Every territorial change carries a recognition set over great powers/blocs. A signed settlement (both belligerents + their patrons) grants recognition: tension from the change decays, occupation converts to ownership/client, costs stop. A unilateral annexation or an armistice-without-treaty leaves the change unrecognized: permanent monthly tension, ideology-pillar penalty (propaganda ammunition for the rival bloc), an open insurgency-funding channel for rivals through the espionage system, and economic-pillar friction (trade/embargo pressure from non-recognizers). Recognition by a specific power is itself negotiable — a diplomatic action purchasable with concessions (recognition of THEIR sphere, trade terms, withdrawal elsewhere), giving the economic and influence pillars a seat at the war-termination table.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Patron veto and third-party stakes in every settlement
mechanics_recommendations.why: HoI4 allies grab land they never fought for because contribution, not stakes, gates the conference; the Cold War inversion is that patrons who did fight (or bankroll) hold vetoes. A Korea settlement the PRC/USSR won't sign is not a settlement — it is an unrecognized occupation with a fuse. This is also the anti-'allies steal land' rule: third parties influence terms, they do not bid for territory.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Each belligerent has zero or more patrons (bloc leaders, intervening powers, major lend-lease sources — derive from existing bloc/relations state). A settlement's acceptance requires patron_acquiescence for every patron above a stakes threshold; acquiescence = f(patron war exhaustion, own escalation risk vs the proposer, side-payments offered, whether the terms touch the patron's declared red lines — e.g. forces on their border). Patrons never receive territory; they receive concessions (recognition, buffer/DMZ provisions, trade). A refused patron converts to the recognition-layer's insurgency/pressure channel or, past a red line, to direct intervention via the existing escalation system.

pitfalls: Do not build a one-shot post-victory conference minigame. Everything wrong with HoI4's system flows from pricing the peace AFTER the war in a separate screen: it invites min-max shopping, divorces war conduct from war aims, and makes the ending anticlimactic. Terms must be continuously priced and offerable during the war so the front line, occupation politics, and patron posture ARE the negotiation.

Do not create a fungible war-score currency spendable on arbitrary territory. The moment points earned anywhere buy provinces anywhere, you get border spaghetti and non-combatants shopping. Bind every claim to concrete provinces justified by occupation, declared war aims, cores, or plebiscites — and let third parties shape terms without ever bidding for land.

Do not make annexation a one-time price. A single up-front cost, however high, is a button players will press; UGS's requirement ('no free annexation') is only met if the cost is ONGOING — non-recognition, insurgency, tension bleed, garrison drain — and only relievable by a settlement someone must actually sign.

Do not let the AI be an inscrutable wall (the EU4 'they never accept anything' failure, and HoI4's opaque bidding). Acceptance math must be deterministic, evaluated on daily/monthly cadence via SimRng forks per the determinism contract, and fully surfaced in the UI: the player should read exactly which term is blocking and what would unblock it. An opaque negotiation is indistinguishable from a broken one.

Do not forget the null outcome is content. An armistice with no treaty (Korea 1953) must be a stable, playable, cost-bearing state — if the design forces every war to a signed settlement, you lose frozen conflicts, which are among the best Cold War stories the game can generate.
analysts.korea_test: USA holds all of North Korea at the Yalu, PRC army intact across the river, war ongoing. Under the recommended system the player sees a settlement panel with priced, offerable term bundles, each with visible acceptance math: (1) STATUS QUO ANTE — withdraw to the 38th; near-zero severity, PRC/DPRK-remnant patrons accept quickly given their exhaustion; rewards are large tension decay, legitimacy/influence gains in the ideology pillar, and full recognition — the cheap, boring, historical exit. (2) NEW LINE / DMZ at the Pyongyang–Wonsan neck — moderate severity; acceptance depends on PRC war exhaustion and Soviet backing; keeps defensible gains, produces a signed alt-history DMZ.
