(3) REUNIFICATION UNDER THE ROK as a US client — high severity: essentially unacceptable while the PRC army stands at the Yalu (patron veto — foreign forces on their border is a red line), so the player's real choices are to buy the veto off (recognize the PRC, concede elsewhere, guarantee US withdrawal south of the neck after transfer to ROK administration) or to keep an UNRECOGNIZED occupation: years of garrison drain, USSR/PRC-funded insurgency in the North (an espionage-pillar battleground), permanent tension bleed, standing Chinese intervention risk — sustainable only if pacification investment (land reform, ROK administration, government-in-exile legitimacy) slowly raises the North's pacification until a later plebiscite or a distracted USSR makes recognition purchasable. (4) UN TRUSTEESHIP over the North — middle path: lower severity because administration is internationalized, costs are shared, tension drops, and a scheduled plebiscite gives a delayed, uncertain reunification. (5) DIRECT US ANNEXATION — never recognized by anyone including allies, priced beyond any acceptance, a propaganda gift to Moscow; possible to attempt unilaterally, ruinous to sustain — exactly the required 'possible but never free.' Meanwhile the world acts: the PRC maintains an intervention posture scaling with how far north US forces sit and whether terms touch its border; the USSR funds resistance in occupied provinces in proportion to non-recognition; neutrals shift influence-pillar alignment against a power that occupies without settling. And if the player simply signs the armistice with no terms — the already-implemented mechanic — the game does not end the story: an unsettled frozen conflict keeps ticking costs on both sides, which is precisely what history did.

findings.title: Limited wars end by freezing, not settling: the armistice is a military document and the peace treaty usually never comes
findings.detail: The Korean Armistice (July 27, 1953) was signed by military commanders — Mark Clark for the UNC, Kim Il-sung and Peng Dehuai for the other side — not by governments. It fixed a Military Demarcation Line and a 4km DMZ, created supervisory machinery (the Military Armistice Commission and the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission), and explicitly deferred all political questions to a conference 'within three months' — the 1954 Geneva Conference, which then failed to produce anything. No Korean peace treaty exists to this day; South Korea never even signed the armistice. The same pattern holds across the era: the 1949 Arab-Israeli armistices produced the Green Line but no peace for 30 years; the 1972 Simla Agreement converted the Kashmir ceasefire line into a 'Line of Control' without resolving sovereignty; the 1973 war ended in disengagement agreements (Sinai I, Jan 1974; Sinai II, Sept 1975), not peace, until Camp David in 1978-79. Design implication: the game's terminal war state should be a first-class 'frozen armistice' — line fixed, claims unresolved, garrisons required, treaty optional and rare — not a settled peace screen.
findings.evidence: Text of the Korean Armistice Agreement (27 July 1953), Article IV para 60; Rosemary Foot, 'A Substitute for Victory: The Politics of Peacemaking at the Korean Armistice Talks' (1990); the 1954 Geneva Conference record; Simla Agreement text (2 July 1972).

findings.title: Talks and fighting run concurrently for one to two years, and the fighting is the bargaining
findings.detail: Korean armistice talks opened at Kaesong on July 10, 1951 — a year into the war — moved to Panmunjom in October 1951, and took two years and 17 days to conclude; roughly 45% of US casualties occurred after negotiations began. The demarcation-line agenda item was settled in November 1951 on the principle of 'line of contact at signature,' which directly incentivized the outpost battles of 1952-53 (Pork Chop Hill, the Chinese offensives of June-July 1953 to bend the line before signing). Vietnam is the extreme case: Paris talks opened May 1968, the agreement came January 27, 1973, and the December 1972 Linebacker II bombing was explicitly a negotiating instrument to force Hanoi back to the table (and to signal resolve to Saigon). Design implication: opening negotiations must not pause the war; the front line at signature should be the settlement line, so late-war offensives have a rational purpose and the player faces the historical grind of fighting for the shape of the ceasefire.
findings.evidence: Foot (1990); Walter Hermes, 'Truce Tent and Fighting Front' (US Army official history of the negotiation-period fighting, 1966); Kissinger, 'White House Years' and 'Ending the Vietnam War' on Linebacker II as coercive diplomacy.

findings.title: The decisive pressure flows patron-to-client, not belligerent-to-belligerent: Suez is the archetype
findings.detail: Suez, Oct 29 - Nov 7, 1956: Britain, France, and Israel were militarily winning and were stopped in nine days by their own superpower patron. Eisenhower blocked IMF support for sterling and let the Treasury signal it might dump sterling bonds during a run on the pound; the US refused emergency oil supplies to Europe (the Saudis had embargoed Britain and France) until withdrawal; the UN General Assembly voted 64-5 under Uniting for Peace on Nov 2; Bulganin sent rocket-rattling letters on Nov 5. Eden accepted a ceasefire Nov 6 and resigned in January 1957. Israel held Sinai until March 1957 and only left under explicit US threat of sanctions (Eisenhower's Feb 20, 1957 television address). The inverse also occurs — patrons shield clients from termination: the USSR vetoed early UNSC ceasefire resolutions in December 1971 to give India time to finish the Bangladesh campaign. And in 1965, the US/UK arms embargo on BOTH India and Pakistan helped end that war in 17 days, with the USSR brokering Tashkent (Jan 10, 1966). Design implication: the game needs patron leverage tools (financial coercion, arms/resupply cutoff, guarantee offers, UN mobilization) usable against allies as well as enemies — and the player must be on the receiving end when they overreach.
findings.evidence: Keith Kyle, 'Suez' (1991); Diane Kunz, 'The Economic Diplomacy of the Suez Crisis' (1991); UNGA Res 997 (Nov 2, 1956); Soviet UNSC vetoes of Dec 4-5, 1971; Tashkent Declaration text.

findings.title: Your own ally is often the biggest obstacle to peace — and must be bought, guaranteed, or coerced
findings.detail: Syngman Rhee opposed any armistice that left Korea divided, demanded a march to the Yalu, and on June 18, 1953 unilaterally released about 27,000 anti-communist North Korean POWs to blow up the nearly-finished agreement. The US response combined a stick — Operation Everready, a drafted contingency plan to remove Rhee by coup — with carrots: the US-ROK Mutual Defense Treaty (signed Oct 1, 1953), long-term economic aid, and a pledge to keep US forces in Korea. Rhee acquiesced but never signed. The identical dynamic ran in Vietnam: Thieu rejected the October 1972 draft ('peace is at hand' collapsed), and Nixon secured his signature with the Enhance Plus arms transfers (Nov 1972), secret letters promising 'swift and severe retaliatory action' if Hanoi violated the accords, and the implicit threat that the US would sign without him. Design implication: client states (a game ROK) need their own war aims and the ability to obstruct — leak terms, refuse to sign, sabotage POW arrangements — resolvable only by paying (defense treaty, aid, guarantees) or coercing (aid cutoff, leadership-removal covert op with legitimacy costs). This is a whole gameplay loop, and it is the player's punishment for total-victory ambitions their patron position can't cash.
findings.evidence: Foot (1990), ch. on Rhee; declassified Operation Everready planning (FRUS 1952-54, Korea, vol. XV); Larry Berman, 'No Peace, No Honor' (2001) on the Nixon-Thieu letters; US-ROK Mutual Defense Treaty (Oct 1, 1953).

findings.title: The sticking points are rarely territory: POWs and symbolic issues consume most of the negotiating time
findings.detail: In Korea, the line was agreed in four months; POW repatriation then stalled the talks for eighteen. The UNC insisted on voluntary repatriation after screening (April 1952) showed only ~70,000 of ~170,000 communist POWs would return — an ideological-warfare victory the US would not trade away, and a humiliation Beijing and Pyongyang could not accept. Talks were suspended entirely from October 1952 to April 1953. The eventual face-saver was a third-party mechanism: the Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission under Indian custodial forces, holding non-repatriates for 90 days of 'explanation' before release. In 1972, India's custody of 93,000 Pakistani POWs was the leverage that shaped Simla. Even procedure becomes a sticking point — the Paris talks spent late 1968 into January 1969 arguing about the shape of the table because seating implied recognition of the NLF and Saigon. Design implication: generate non-territorial agenda items (POWs, foreign-troop withdrawal, recognition/status of regimes) that can each deadlock independently, and provide face-saving third-party instruments (neutral commissions, UN peacekeepers like UNEF, created Nov 1956 as the first ever) that unlock deadlocks at a diplomatic price.
findings.evidence: Foot (1990); the armistice's NNRC terms of reference; screening figures in Hermes (1966); Simla negotiation accounts (P.N. Dhar); Paris talks procedural record, Nov 1968-Jan 1969.

findings.title: Deadlocks break via external shocks — leadership change and superpower confrontation — not smooth attrition
findings.detail: The Korean POW deadlock broke within weeks of Stalin's death (March 5, 1953): the new Soviet leadership signaled flexibility, China accepted the sick-and-wounded exchange (Little Switch, April 1953), and the armistice followed in July. Eisenhower's election (Nov 1952) and his hints of escalation changed the US side's calculus the same winter. The other great unblocker is superpower near-collision under the nuclear shadow: on Oct 24-25, 1973, Brezhnev's letter threatening unilateral Soviet intervention to save the encircled Egyptian Third Army triggered a US DEFCON 3 alert — and within 48 hours the US forced ISRAEL, its own ally, to halt and allow supply convoys through to the trapped army. When patrons touch, wars end in days; the 1967 war also ended in six days with the Washington-Moscow hotline used operationally for the first time. Design implication: negotiation stall states should persist until event-driven shocks (leader death/succession, election, escalation-ladder contact between superpowers) rather than ticking down a visible timer — and direct superpower contact should trigger a compressed forced-termination sequence measured in days, imposing terms on clients on both sides.
findings.evidence: Kathryn Weathersby's Cold War International History Project work on Soviet documents post-Stalin; FRUS 1952-54 Korea on Little Switch; Kissinger, 'Years of Upheaval' and the Oct 24-25, 1973 DEFCON 3 record; hotline use June 1967.

findings.title: Conquest kept is conquest paid for forever; status quo ante is the modal imposed outcome
findings.detail: Across 1945-1990, wholesale keeping of conquered territory essentially never received recognition. Tashkent (1966) and Simla (1972) returned captured territory in the West both times; Suez forced full withdrawal twice over (Nov 1956 - March 1957); Israel kept its 1967 conquests only as unrecognized occupations requiring permanent mobilization, and converting even one of them (Sinai) into recognized peace cost the entire peninsula plus roughly $2B/year in US aid to each signatory after 1979. The one 'successful' regime-replacement — India creating Bangladesh in 1971 — worked because it installed an independent successor state, took 13 days, was shielded by a Soviet veto umbrella, and India still returned the Western territory and the POWs. The precedent for the player's exact position is grim: the US decision to cross the 38th parallel (authorized late Sept 1950, NSC 81/1) and drive to the Yalu, dismissing Zhou Enlai's Oct 3, 1950 warning passed through Indian ambassador Panikkar, converted a won limited war into a two-and-a-half-year superpower-adjacent war. Design implication: restoring the status quo ante should be the cheap, fast, tension-reducing option; each step beyond it (new line, regime change, absorption) should cost more in patron relations, neutral alignment, occupation burden, and escalation risk — superlinearly.
findings.evidence: NSC 81/1 (Sept 1950); Allen Whiting, 'China Crosses the Yalu' (1960) on the Panikkar warning; Tashkent and Simla texts; Egypt-Israel treaty (1979) aid figures; Chen Jian, 'China's Road to the Korean War' (1994).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Armistice conference as a persistent, multi-agenda negotiation object that runs while the war continues
mechanics_recommendations.why: Every major limited war of the era ended through months-to-years of talks-during-fighting, with independent agenda items (line, POWs, foreign forces, political status) each able to deadlock. A single 'accept armistice' bool cannot represent Korea; the current 10-months-war + 2-months-static trigger should become the condition for OPENING talks, not ending the war.
mechanics_recommendations.how: State: a `PeaceConference` entity per war with agenda items, each holding both sides' positions (e.g. Line: {StatusQuoAnte, CurrentLine, NamedLine(province set)}; POWs: {AllRepatriated, VoluntaryRepatriation}; ForeignForces: {Withdraw, Remain}; PoliticalStatus: {RestoreRegime, NewLine, UnifiedUnder(tag), Trusteeship, Puppet(tag)}). Talks open when both sides' willingness crosses the existing threshold. Each item resolves when concession pressure (war weariness + front movement against you + patron pressure + shock events) exceeds that item's stubbornness; POW/status items get high stubbornness so they deadlock realistically for months. Signature requires all items resolved; the territorial line is sampled AT SIGNATURE, so late offensives matter. Monthly cadence off `SimClock::new_month`, all randomness via `rng.fork(b"peace_talks")`.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Patron leverage: coercion and shielding along the patron-client axis, targeting allies as well as enemies
mechanics_recommendations.why: Suez, Vietnam, 1965, and 1973 all ended because a superpower squeezed (or stopped shielding) a client — often its own. This is the mechanism that makes 'no free annexation' real: the player's patron position gives tools, and overreach makes the player the target of the enemy patron's counter-mobilization and even their own coalition's defection.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Actions available to a patron toward a belligerent it supplies/backs: cut arms resupply (client combat effectiveness decays over weeks), financial coercion (drains client treasury/stability — the sterling squeeze), offer a guarantee package (defense treaty + aid, buys acceptance of terms the client hates), or mobilize the UN (world-opinion penalty per month the target fights on). Each action costs relations/influence and is visible to the world. Inverse: a patron can veto/shield (blocks UN pressure, at tension cost — the 1971 Soviet veto). AI patrons apply these automatically when a war threatens escalation ladder contact or their client is being erased. Numbers live in a `tuning` module per convention.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Client obstruction: allied belligerents have their own war aims and can sabotage a settlement (the Rhee/Thieu loop)
mechanics_recommendations.why: The hardest, most game-worthy politics of war termination in 1953 and 1972-73 was managing one's OWN ally. It converts 'I won, give me everything' into a dilemma even when the enemy is beaten: your client wants more than the world will let you take, or less than you want to give away.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Each belligerent client gets a `WarAims` component (e.g. ROK: UnifiedUnder(ROK)). When a draft settlement falls short of its aims, the client accumulates `Obstruction` monthly; past thresholds it fires sabotage events (unilateral POW release, offensive without authorization, public denunciation) that reset resolved agenda items or spike enemy stubbornness. The patron player clears obstruction by: guarantee package (defense treaty entity + aid commitment, permanent upkeep), aid-cutoff threat (works but drops client stability/loyalty), or a covert leadership-removal op through the existing espionage pillar (Everready — fast, but legitimacy and world-opinion costs, and a failure risk that wrecks the alliance). The client never signs if unappeased — the armistice can still bind (Rhee didn't sign) but the unappeased client keeps generating border-incident flashpoints afterward.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Frozen-armistice end state: DMZ entity, no treaty, unresolved claims as a permanent stable condition
mechanics_recommendations.why: The armistice-without-peace is not a missing feature of the era, it IS the era's signature outcome (Korea, Kashmir, the Golan). The game must let a war 'end' into a 40-year frozen conflict that stays playable: garrison costs, flashpoints, and a later diplomatic path to a real treaty.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Signing creates an `Armistice` entity: the MDL province set, a DMZ strip (provinces demilitarized — units entering trigger violations), required garrison levels on both sides (undermanning invites probe events), and a supervisory commission flag that damps flashpoint frequency. Claims remain: the map shows de facto control distinct from de jure recognition (a per-country recognition set, defaulting to non-recognition of any war-transferred territory). A separate, rare `PeaceTreaty` action converts armistice to peace — requires major concessions (land-for-peace: return territory, à la Sinai) or a generational relations shift, and only a treaty grants recognition, ends occupation penalties, and lets tension from that dyad fully decay.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Shock-driven deadlock breaking and the superpower compression clock
mechanics_recommendations.why: Korea's endgame was unblocked by Stalin's death, not by a timer; 1973 ended in 48 hours once DEFCON 3 hit. Deterministic countdowns players can read make negotiation gamey; event shocks make it historical and replayable, and direct superpower contact should slam wars shut fast — reinforcing the escalation pillar.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Concession pressure gets a large one-time delta from typed shocks: leader death/succession in a belligerent or patron (roll monthly from `rng.fork(b"succession")` against age/stability tables), election turnover in democracies (already-datable), and nuclear-signaling events from the existing escalation system. Separately, if patron great powers' own forces enter direct combat or a nuclear alert fires during a proxy war, spawn a `ForcedTermination` sequence: both patrons impose the current line on their clients within N days (N small, 2-7), skipping unresolved agenda items (they become frozen disputes on the armistice entity). Refusing your patron's imposition as a client is possible but severs the patronage.

pitfalls: The HoI4/EU4 'peace conference screen' trap: a post-war shopping menu where warscore buys provinces makes annexation a linear price instead of a categorically different act. Historically termination was a process DURING the war (2 years at Panmunjom, 5 at Paris), and outright absorption of a conquered state by a superpower simply has no 1945-1990 precedent — the design should make it possible only via the puppet/reunification-under-client path, never as a direct 'transfer to me' line item.

Modeling pressure only between the belligerents. Most real termination leverage ran patron-to-client (Eisenhower vs. Eden, Nixon vs. Thieu, US vs. Rhee, US vs. Israel on Oct 25, 1973, USSR shielding India in 1971). If the game only tracks enemy-vs-enemy willingness, it cannot reproduce a single one of the era's actual war endings.

Treating armistice as peace: auto-settling borders, dissolving claims, or ending occupation state at signature. The unresolved frozen conflict must be stable, cheap enough to live with, and permanent-by-default — Korea has now been in armistice for 70+ years. If the engine demands a 'final' territorial settlement to close a war, the signature outcome of the whole era becomes unrepresentable.

Readable deterministic timers ('AI signs after X months') that players min-max. Real durations were driven by which sticking point deadlocked and which external shock broke it (Stalin's death, elections, DEFCON alerts). Keep the OPENING of talks threshold-based, but make RESOLUTION event- and pressure-driven, with the deadlock item visible but its break date not.

Pricing overreach only in resources. Holding all of North Korea shouldn't just cost money and manpower — it must move the world: neutral alignment drift toward the other bloc, enemy-patron intervention risk, your own coalition's cohesion dropping, UN resolutions stacking. Suez cost Britain its great-power standing, not merely sterling reserves; a gold-only cost invites the player to simply pay it.

Forgetting the client's veto in the other direction: if the player can always sign for their whole side, the Rhee/Thieu dynamic vanishes. But also don't make obstruction a hard wall — the US signed at Panmunjom without Rhee's signature. Obstruction should degrade and complicate settlements, not deadlock the game.
analysts.korea_test: The player's position — USA holding all of North Korea at the Yalu with the PRC engaged — is precisely the position MacArthur sought in October-November 1950, and history's verdict is that it is a maximally unstable salient, not a victory to bank. The system should present it as an ongoing auction under pressure, not a prize screen. Concretely: (1) Talks open at Panmunjom-style conference once willingness thresholds are met, with the war continuing; the line item defaults to 'line of contact at signature,' so the PRC AI keeps launching offensives to bend the Yalu line while talking — as China did in June-July 1953. (2) The settlement menu, priced steeply upward: restore the 38th parallel status quo ante (fast PRC/USSR acceptance, large tension decay, DPRK restored as a rump — the cheap out); a new line at the peninsula's narrow neck (Pyongyang-Wonsan) creating a smaller DPRK (requires months of deadlock, heavy PRC war-weariness, and either a Soviet-side shock like Stalin's death or US patron-leverage spend); reunification under ROK (requires the PRC army broken or Soviet patronage withdrawn — an event-gated outcome, and even then it terminates as an ARMISTICE with the PRC across the Yalu, never a recognized treaty: permanent Yalu garrison requirement facing China, northern resistance/partisan events, reconstruction drain, USSR tension spike, and neutral-bloc alignment drift against the US for years); UN trusteeship of the North (face-saving middle path — moderate upkeep, defers final status, later plebiscite events, the historical 1945-48 trusteeship idea resurrected). Direct annexation to the USA is not on the menu at all — no such option existed in the era's diplomacy, and its absence IS the design statement. (3) The Rhee mechanic runs throughout: ROK's war aim is reunification, so every option short of it accumulates Obstruction — expect a unilateral POW-release sabotage event mid-talks (June 18, 1953 analog) unless the player pre-empts with a Mutual Defense Treaty + aid package (permanent commitments) or an Everready-style covert removal (espionage-pillar op, legitimacy cost, alliance risk). Conversely, if the player pushes reunification, the obstruction runs on the OTHER patron's side and the escalation pillar takes over. (4) The AI/world response: USSR shields its clients with UN vetoes and threatens intervention as the player's position hardens; neutral nations drift; if US and Soviet forces ever touch directly or a nuclear alert fires, the ForcedTermination clock compresses everything to days and both superpowers impose the current line on their clients — the player included. (5) POW repatriation should be the generated sticking point that stalls the conference 6-18 game-months unless conceded, teaching the player that in limited war the last mile is never about the map. Expected historical-baseline outcome if the player just waits: 12-24 months of fighting-while-talking, an armistice near the best defensible line they can actually hold, a DMZ entity, no treaty, and a frozen conflict they garrison for the rest of the century — which is the game's thesis working as intended.

analysts.analyst: alt-history-endstates (game-design analyst: earned divergence, war termination, settlement spaces)

findings.title: Divergence feels earned when the ending is the resolution of tracked pressures, not a menu pick
findings.detail: The core difference between CK-style emergent alt-history and HoI4 focus-tree alt-history is authorship: in CK the world state you end with is readable back through causes you lived through, while focus trees hand you pre-written endings that feel identical across runs. For war termination this means the settlement system should never present 'endings' as options that appear when war score hits N; it should present clauses whose availability is computed from facts the player created (where the armies stand, whose patron is committed, what the UN blessed). A reunified Korea should be narratable afterward as 'possible because China's intervention broke on the Chongchon and Moscow was distracted by the succession crisis' — the game tracking those gates is what makes the outcome feel earned. HoI4's own designers conceded their old take-what-you-want conference was among the game's most disliked features and rebuilt it around simultaneous bidding precisely because sequential free-taking produced arbitrary, unearned maps. Twilight Struggle gets 'earned' a third way: nothing is ever taken, regions are scored repeatedly, so every position is only as good as your continuing ability to defend it — a model for making post-war Korea stay contested rather than frozen.
findings.evidence: HoI4 'By Blood Alone' peace conference rework rationale (simultaneous bidding, contested-state cost inflation, fixed points from war participation): https://hoi4.paradoxwikis.com/By_Blood_Alone and the Paradox Designer Corner: Peace Conference thread (https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/developer-diary/designer-corner-peace-conference.1523321/page-5). Twilight Struggle's repeated region scoring as anti-freeze design. CK3's emergent-narrative reputation vs the standard critique of HoI4 alt-history paths as railroaded.

findings.title: The end-state space for a Korea-like war is small, enumerable, and should be gated on three independent axes: military facts, patron consent, international legitimacy
findings.detail: For Korea the plausible settlement templates are: (1) status quo ante (restore the 38th parallel); (2) new line/DMZ at or near the line of control (the historical 1953 outcome); (3) reunification under the South; (4) reunification under the North; (5) neutralized unified Korea on the Austria 1955 model (unification bought with bloc exclusion); (6) UN trusteeship/interim administration (the actual 1945 Moscow Conference plan — four-power trusteeship up to five years — and UNTCOK/UNCURK machinery); (7) partition into occupation zones on the German model; (8) rump state (a Pusan-perimeter ROK or a Yalu-pocket DPRK surviving as a revanchist remnant). The same grammar covers a Germany crisis (status quo, reunification either way, neutralized unified Germany per the 1952 Stalin Note, four-power condominium) and Indochina (colonial restoration, partition at a parallel per Geneva 1954, unified state either direction, neutralization per Laos 1962). Each template should be a bundle of clauses, and each clause checks the three axes separately: you cannot hold territory you don't occupy or can't plausibly defend (military), you cannot extinguish a client state whose patron is undefeated and unconsenting (patron consent — this is why total-victory-over-the-client settles nothing), and sovereignty-transferring clauses need legitimacy cover or they price out in tension. Three independent gates is what makes eight endings reachable without any of them being free.
findings.evidence: Moscow Conference (Dec 1945) four-power trusteeship plan for Korea; UN resolution of 7 Oct 1950 endorsing 'a unified, independent and democratic Korea' (the legitimacy instrument the US actually held when crossing the parallel); Austrian State Treaty 1955 (unification-for-neutrality trade); Stalin Note March 1952 (neutralized unified Germany offer); Geneva Conference 1954 (Indochina partition at the 17th; its Korea phase failed to produce a treaty).

findings.title: Cold War proxy wars end when patrons let clients settle — patrons must sit at the table, and conquering the client without patron consent converts war into a standing crisis
findings.detail: The Korean armistice took two years of talking (Kaesong then Panmunjom, July 1951–July 1953) not because the line was contested but because of clause-level disputes (voluntary POW repatriation above all) and because Stalin was content to let the war bleed the US; the logjam broke within months of his death in March 1953. And China entered the war in the first place precisely because the US drove for the Yalu — NSC-81/1 had explicitly conditioned crossing the 38th on no Soviet or Chinese intervention, a real-world 'patron consent gate' Washington wrote down and then ignored. Mechanically: every war should carry a stakeholder set larger than its belligerents — patrons, and optionally the UN — and clauses that touch a client's existence (annexation, regime replacement, unification) require the relevant patron to accept, be defeated, or be strategically distracted. If the gate fails, the best available result downgrades to armistice-at-the-line: a frozen conflict, not a settlement. This is also the natural hook into the game's other pillars — patron consent can be bought with concessions elsewhere (escalation pillar), manufactured via a distracted patron (espionage/influence), or priced in brinkmanship risk.
findings.evidence: Armistice negotiation history: agenda fights at Kaesong/Panmunjom 1951-53, POW repatriation as the 18-month sticking point, movement after Stalin's death (March–July 1953); NSC-81/1 (Sept 1950) conditioning the crossing of the 38th; Chinese warnings via Zhou Enlai/Panikkar (Oct 1950) before intervention.

findings.title: Price outcomes superlinearly and in multiple currencies — one war-score number always recreates the 'take everything' button
findings.detail: Every game that priced peace in a single fungible currency rediscovered the same exploit: grind to max score, buy the map (HoI4 pre-1.12, EU4 before aggressive-expansion/coalitions had teeth). The fixes that worked are (a) convex cost in distance-from-status-quo — the second province costs more than the first, extinguishing a state costs categorically more than border adjustment — and (b) heterogeneous currencies that don't convert: military position buys lines, legitimacy buys sovereignty transfers, domestic political capital buys the war lasting long enough, and world tension is a cost you pay rather than a resource you spend. Victoria 3's diplomatic plays put the price tag at demand time — adding an aggressive demand immediately generates infamy before a shot is fired — which is worth copying: declaring 'unification' as your war aim mid-war should itself cost tension and harden the enemy coalition, so ambition is priced continuously, not settled at the end. Status quo ante should be near-free or even pay a small legitimacy dividend, because that asymmetry is what makes restraint a strategy rather than a concession screen.
findings.evidence: HoI4 BBA contested-state cost inflation and fixed participation-based points (https://hoi4.paradoxwikis.com/By_Blood_Alone); Victoria 3 Dev Diary #21 — aggressive demands generate infamy at declaration, war as continuation of diplomacy (https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/developer-diary/victoria-3-dev-diary-21-diplomatic-plays.1495892/); EU4 aggressive expansion/coalition system as the genre's standard superlinear brake on conquest.

findings.title: The settlement must instantiate live aftermath objects — revanchism, frozen conflicts, refugee demographics, alignment shifts — or alt-history is just map paint
findings.detail: The player should feel the difference between endings for the rest of the campaign, which means every settlement writes persistent objects into the world, not just province ownership. A rump state keeps cores and generates a RevanchistClaim that spawns periodic border crises and gives the loser's patron a cheap influence lever (the actual DPRK post-1953: DMZ raids, the 1968 Blue House raid, a 70-year armistice that never became peace). An imposed reunification generates an occupation/consolidation phase with garrison and reconstruction costs plus patron-sponsored insurgency in the absorbed half. A neutralization settlement removes the country from both blocs' influence scoring (Austria/Finland effect) — cheap to get consent for, expensive in strategic position. Refugee flows are the demographic teeth: the Korean War displaced millions southward (the Hungnam evacuation alone moved ~100,000 civilians), and modeling that shifts province demographics, creates short-term unrest and long-term ideological sorting — the game already has a demography system to receive it. Twilight Struggle's lesson applies at campaign scale: a settled region should still be scoreable, so a 'won' Korea remains a place where the Cold War happens.
findings.evidence: Post-armistice Korea as permanent frozen conflict (no peace treaty after Geneva 1954; DMZ incidents through the whole Cold War); Hungnam evacuation Dec 1950 and mass southward refugee flows 1950-53; Austrian State Treaty/Finlandization as bloc-exclusion aftermath; Twilight Struggle repeated scoring keeping 'settled' regions live; existing project docs docs/design/systems/demography.md and influence.md as the receiving systems.

findings.title: Armistice and peace are different objects — the two-stage model is a gift to a Cold War game, because frozen conflicts are content, not failure
findings.detail: Korea teaches that ceasefire (military document, signed by commanders, freezes a line) and settlement (political document, signed by states, disposes of sovereignty) are separable, and the gap between them can last decades. The game already has armistice-at-the-line implemented; the design move is to make that stage one, which creates a FrozenConflict object — tension floor, DMZ garrison upkeep on both sides, re-ignition triggers, and a standing diplomatic item that can be converted into a real settlement years later when the gates finally open (patron dies, regime changes, exhaustion accumulates). This resolves the current dead-end elegantly: the player on the Yalu who cannot get Chinese/Soviet consent doesn't hit a wall, they hold an expensive, tense, legally unresolved occupation — historically exactly what an armistice there would have been — and the campaign continues with that as a live problem and opportunity. It also matches the vision doc's thesis: the game is about managing unresolved confrontation, not closing it out.
findings.evidence: Korean Armistice Agreement (27 July 1953) signed by military commanders only, ROK never signed; Geneva 1954's failure to convert it to a peace treaty; parallel cases: Kashmir 1949 ceasefire line, Taiwan Strait's unterminated civil war. Current implementation state per task brief (armistice at line of control exists; everything after it is missing).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Settlement proposals as clause bundles (with named historical templates)
mechanics_recommendations.why: Eight end states cannot each be a hardcoded 'ending'; they must be points in one composable space so hybrids emerge (a new line PLUS demilitarization PLUS a trusteeship over the gap). Templates give the AI evaluable packages and give the player historical legibility, while the clause grammar keeps outcomes systemic rather than authored.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Data: `Clause` enum — BorderChange(line spec: status-quo-ante | line-of-control | named line), SovereigntyTransfer(target, to: annex|puppet|new-state), Unification(under), Neutralization(country, duration), Trusteeship(admin: UN|powers, review_date), Demilitarization(zone, depth_km), Recognition(state), Reparations(amount), PopulationTransfer/POWRepatriation(mode), RegimeChange(target, ideology). `SettlementTemplate` = named Vec<Clause> defined in RON (assets/data), e.g. `status_quo_ante`, `new_dmz`, `unification_south`, `neutralized_unification`, `un_trusteeship`, `partition`. State: `ActiveNegotiation { war_id, proposal: Vec<Clause>, proposer, round: u32, stakeholder_responses: BTreeMap<CountryTag, Response> }` living in the Resolve stage. Each clause carries: cost vector (see pricing mechanic), gate predicates (see acceptance mechanic), and an `aftermath` spec naming the objects it instantiates.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Three-gate stakeholder acceptance model (military facts, patron consent, legitimacy)
mechanics_recommendations.why: This is what makes big outcomes possible-but-not-free and small outcomes attractive. It also replaces the current binary 'both sides willing' armistice check with something the player can read and work: each stakeholder's ledger shows WHY they refuse, which turns diplomacy into gameplay (change the fact, flip the gate).
mechanics_recommendations.how: Stakeholder set per war = belligerents ∪ patrons(belligerents) ∪ {UN if resolution active}. Per stakeholder compute `U_settle = Σ clause_utility(clause, stakeholder)` and `U_continue = expected_line_shift(force ratios, trend of front movement over last 60 days) − exhaustion_rate × horizon − escalation_risk(tension, nuclear posture)`; accept when U_settle > U_continue + stubbornness(regime type, domestic politics). Hard gates on top of utility: (1) MILITARY — a BorderChange clause is only offerable for territory currently occupied or within a small negotiable band of the line of control; (2) PATRON — SovereigntyTransfer/Unification/RegimeChange clauses against a client require its patron's acceptance, OR patron at war and losing, OR patron `distraction ≥ threshold` (fed by espionage/crisis systems); failing this gate greys the clause and offers armistice-only as the fallback; (3) LEGITIMACY — clauses above a sovereignty-weight threshold require `legitimacy_points ≥ cost`, earned via UN resolutions, coalition breadth (16-nation-UN-command analog), and enemy-first-aggression, spent at signing. Exhaustion accumulates from casualties/duration exactly as the current 10-month heuristic implies, but per-stakeholder. Patrons' utilities count bloc position, not territory — Moscow can prefer a bleeding stalemate (Stalin 1951-52) until a leadership-transition event drops its stubbornness (Stalin-death analog as a systemic event, not a script).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Convex, multi-currency clause pricing declared at demand time
mechanics_recommendations.why: Kills the 'win the war, take everything' button structurally: no single number can buy annexation, and ambition costs from the moment it is declared (Victoria 3's infamy-at-demand insight), so a player driving for unification pays in hardened enemy resolve and world tension all war long, not in a lump at the end.
mechanics_recommendations.how: Each clause has cost vector (war_position, tension, legitimacy, political_capital). Total sovereignty weight of a proposal `W = Σ w_i` (border tweak w=1, new DMZ w=2, puppet w=4, unification w=8, annexation-into-self w=12); tension cost = base × W^1.5, so unification costs ~8× a border tweak, not 4×. War aims are declared and revisable mid-war: raising aims (38th → Yalu → unification) triggers an immediate tension increment, hardens all enemy-side stubbornness, and historically models the Oct 1950 overreach; lowering aims refunds nothing but softens stubbornness. Contested clauses (both sides demand the same disposition) inflate 10%/negotiation round, per HoI4 BBA. Status quo ante has W=0: near-zero cost, small legitimacy dividend to the defender's side. All constants live in a `tuning` module / RON data per project convention.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Aftermath objects: RevanchistClaim, FrozenConflict, NeutralizationPact, OccupationAuthority, RefugeeFlow
mechanics_recommendations.why: The settlement must write into the ongoing simulation or alt-history is cosmetic. These five objects make every ending feel different for decades of game time and give the influence/espionage/tension pillars new terrain — a rump DPRK is a crisis generator, a neutralized Korea is a scoring hole, an occupied North is a bleeding cost with a consolidation payoff.
mechanics_recommendations.how: `RevanchistClaim { holder, target_provinces, intensity }`: loser keeps cores on lost land; intensity decays ~2%/year but spikes on anniversaries/crises; feeds a flashpoint system (border incidents, patron aid, future casus belli). `FrozenConflict { line, parties, since }`: created by armistice-without-treaty; imposes DMZ garrison upkeep scaling with line length and opposing force size, a regional tension floor, and a standing 'convene peace conference' diplomatic action whose gates are re-evaluated monthly. `NeutralizationPact { country, guarantors }`: country excluded from both blocs' influence targeting; violation by any guarantor = major tension spike + free legitimacy to the other bloc. `OccupationAuthority { zone, kind: MilitaryGov|Trusteeship|ClientAdmin, cost/mo, resistance }`: resistance driven by ideology distance × wartime conduct × foreign sponsorship (patron-funded insurgency via espionage pillar); consolidation completes after N years of resistance below threshold, converting occupation into real sovereignty — expensive but real, so annexation is a project, not a click. `RefugeeFlow { from_zone, to_zone, size, ideology_profile }`: moves population between provinces via the demography system, short-term unrest at destination, long-term ideological sorting (the historical southward flight hardening the South's anticommunism).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Negotiation as a real-time process, not a modal screen
mechanics_recommendations.why: The Panmunjom lesson: talking while fighting IS the endgame gameplay, and it fits real-time-with-pause far better than a HoI4-style conference popup. Fighting during talks moves the offerable line (the 1951 line-of-contact agreement made the front static because both sides stopped bidding with blood); clause disputes (POW repatriation) consume months — that pacing is the drama.
mechanics_recommendations.how: A proposed settlement opens a negotiation running on the weekly cadence (`SimClock::new_day`-derived flags per project convention): each round, stakeholders respond per the acceptance model, contested clauses inflate, and battlefield changes since last round shift utilities (a captured hill literally moves the negotiable band). Either side can fight-while-talking; breaking off talks costs the breaker legitimacy. AI proposes too: an exhausted enemy tables its own template (e.g. PRC offers new-line-at-38th), forcing the player to accept, counter, or visibly refuse peace — refusal is public and priced in tension and domestic political capital.

pitfalls: Single-currency war score. If one number buys everything, optimal play is grind-to-100-then-annex and the forbidden 'win the war get everything' button reappears wearing a different UI. Currencies must be non-convertible: military position can never substitute for patron consent or legitimacy.

A menu of authored endings. If 'Reunify Korea' is an option that lights up at a threshold, every campaign converges on the same three buttons and the alt-history feels like HoI4 focus-tree railroading. Endings must be compositions of clauses whose gates are computed from world state, so hybrid and asymmetric outcomes appear that the designers never named.

Occupation as pure punishment. If holding conquered land is only unrest-whack-a-mole with no consolidation path, rational players stop at the armistice every time and the big alt-history outcomes become theoretically possible but never chosen. There must be an expensive, multi-year, failure-prone but REAL path to making gains stick.

Opaque AI acceptance. 'The enemy refuses your proposal' with no ledger teaches the player nothing and reads as random; every stakeholder's gates and utility deltas must be inspectable so refusal becomes a puzzle (flip the gate) rather than a dice roll. This is also a determinism asset: the ledger is pure state.

Settlements that don't write back into the political map. The current frozen province->occupier table is a dead end: if a settlement can't create new countries, puppets, cores, and pacts as first-class sim objects, alt-history can't compound — a unified Korea in 1952 must be a real country that participates in the 1960s, not paint.

Scripting the divergence points. Modeling Stalin's death or Chinese intervention as scripted events makes the alt-history gates feel like waiting for a timer; both should be systemic (leadership-transition risk, intervention-commitment thresholds) so different campaigns get different keys to the same doors.
analysts.korea_test: Situation: USA occupies all of North Korea, holds the Yalu, PRC glowering across the river. Under this design the player opens a negotiation (weekly cadence, fighting optional) and finds a clause space with per-stakeholder ledgers — DPRK-remnant, PRC (patron/belligerent), USSR (patron, not formally at war), ROK, UN. Options and prices: (1) STATUS QUO ANTE — restore the 38th, W=0: PRC and USSR accept almost immediately (their client survives intact), tension drops, US banks a legitimacy dividend and a restored-but-hostile DPRK with a RevanchistClaim on nothing; domestic political capital takes a hit ('we marched to the Yalu for this?') — cheap, safe, historically the pre-intervention off-ramp NSC-81/1 gestured at. (2) NEW LINE at the Pyongyang–Wonsan narrow neck — W~2: offerable because the US occupies it; PRC accepts only if its expected-line-shift calculation says intervention can't do better (i.e., the player has visibly fortified and PRC commitment is not yet total); result is a rump DPRK with intense revanchism, a FrozenConflict object, and permanent DMZ upkeep — the 'greedy but survivable' outcome. (3) REUNIFICATION UNDER THE ROK — W=8, the big prize, and all three gates bind: military (survive the Chinese counterblow with the line intact — holding the Yalu on day one is necessary, not sufficient), patron consent (USSR/PRC must accept, which at full commitment they won't — the player needs a systemic key: Soviet leadership transition, a crisis elsewhere consuming Moscow, or brinkmanship that raises escalation_risk in THEIR continue-utility, each with its own dangers), and legitimacy (a UN resolution analog to Oct 7 1950 plus UN-supervised-elections clause, cheaper if the war stays multilateral). Even signed, it instantiates an OccupationAuthority over the north for years — garrison costs, PRC-sponsored insurgency via the espionage layer, refugee churn — before consolidation makes it real; PRC keeps a RevanchistClaim and the Yalu becomes a militarized frontier feeding the tension floor for decades. (4) UN TRUSTEESHIP over the north — W~4 but legitimacy-priced rather than tension-priced: hands the zone to a UNCURK-style authority, slashes occupation costs and tension, defers final status to an elections event years out whose result is decided by the influence pillar — the patient player's route to unification. (5) NEUTRALIZED UNIFIED KOREA (Austria model) — W=8 but with a Neutralization clause that pays most of the bill: Moscow and Beijing consent far more readily because the US trades away bases and bloc membership; Korea leaves the US influence map permanently — unification bought with strategic position. If the player instead just sits on the Yalu offering nothing, the world acts: PRC intervention commitment ticks up monthly (crossing-the-river becomes likelier the longer the humiliation stands), USSR feeds MiGs and advisors short of formal entry, world tension rises on the occupation itself, third countries drift on 'US expansionism,' and US domestic political capital bleeds with war exhaustion. And if talks genuinely deadlock — patron consent unreachable, both sides exhausted — the fallback is the armistice the game already has, now upgraded into a FrozenConflict: the US administers all of North Korea indefinitely, legally unresolved, garrisoned against a hostile China, expensive every single month. Every one of the player's requested alt-histories is reachable; none of them, including doing nothing, is free."

findings.title: Prices players can pay in a currency conquest replenishes are speed bumps; consent held by an AI actor is not
findings.detail: Every genre penalty that is a mere price gets routed around: EU4 AE is regionally scoped and decays on a clock, and the coalition threat it feeds is defeated by truce-timer juggling (declare well-timed wars so potential coalition members are always under truce and ineligible) — the community itself names this the biggest exploit and calls it 'game-y and immersion breaking'. Deeper failure: EU4's conquest pays for the tools that manage its own penalty (more dev, more armies, admin efficiency), which is why 'wide is always right' there. The exploit-proof alternative is to make the constraint a DECISION by a named actor with its own state: the war does not legally end until the defeated side's patron (PRC/USSR) signs, and their signature is a function of what you demand, what you offer, and where your troops stand. You cannot juggle timers against a veto; you can only compensate it, defeat it at horrific tension cost, or live without a real peace. This converts the anti-exploit guard from arithmetic into gameplay that runs on the game's existing pillars (tension, influence, intel).
findings.evidence: EU4 truce/coalition exploit threads: [Paradox forum — coalition system](https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/simple-change-to-the-coalition-system.1713197/), [truce timers ruining games](https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/is-there-any-way-to-prevent-truce-timers-from-ruining-your-game.838122/), [Steam AE discussion](https://steamcommunity.com/app/236850/discussions/0/2741975115079174399/). Historically: the Korean armistice required two years of talks-under-fire precisely because settlement needed Chinese/Soviet consent, not just battlefield facts.

findings.title: Time-decay as the universal solvent is the Vic3 infamy failure; discharge must come through play
findings.detail: Vic3 infamy accumulates smoothly and gates a sharp pariah threshold at 100, but its only sink is waiting — so the dominant strategy is 'conquer, idle, conquer', and the tuning oscillates between toothless and game-saying-no (players report waiting '20% of the game timeline' for infamy from three small regions to fade, and that the system 'tries to block wars entirely'). Civ's warmonger penalty is the opposite extreme: near-eternal, opaque, and it punishes defenders, so it reads as unfair nagging rather than a constraint — which is why Firaxis replaced it with legible, per-civ, negotiable grievances. Lesson for UGS: every settlement cost must be dischargeable through actions (compensate the patron elsewhere, sponsor détente, accept UN supervision, liberate rather than hold), decay only conditionally (good behavior, honored terms), and be per-actor — the PRC cares intensely about the Yalu, Brazil does not.
findings.evidence: [Vic3 infamy poorly balanced — Paradox forum](https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/infamy-is-poorly-balanced.1692886/), [Steam: fix infamy](https://steamcommunity.com/app/529340/discussions/0/3828664382482507147/); Civ 6 warmonger criticism: [penalty needs revision](https://steamcommunity.com/app/289070/discussions/0/2381701715721118959/), [warmonger as defender](https://steamcommunity.com/app/289070/discussions/0/143387886725128983/).

findings.title: Capacity constraints resist exploits better than prices; occupation must be an ongoing bleed, not a lump sum
findings.detail: Terra Invicta's control-point cap is the genre's cleanest anti-wide mechanic: you literally cannot hold more nations than your administrative capacity supports without everything degrading, and raising the cap is itself a strategic investment. Prices get optimized; capacities force portfolio choices. For UGS the fictional grounding is perfect: occupation garrisons drawing continuously on the military stockpile and manpower pipeline (already implemented), scaled by occupied population and resistance level, mean 'annex everything' is not a fee paid once at the peace table but a permanent line item competing with the arms race — the economic-competition pillar taxing the conquest pillar forever. HoI4's own peace-conference redesign concedes the companion point: the old winner-takes-all locked-claim model produced absurd outcomes, and the fix was contestable claims where other powers get a seat — i.e., spoils became negotiated, not clicked.
findings.evidence: [Terra Invicta control point capacity — official wiki](https://wiki.hoodedhorse.com/Terra_Invicta/Control_Point_Capacity), [Steam CP cap discussions](https://steamcommunity.com/app/1176470/discussions/0/3361398331720571898/); [HoI4 Designer Corner: Peace Conference](https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/developer-diary/designer-corner-peace-conference.1523321/page-5), [HoI4 wiki: peace conference](https://hoi4.paradoxwikis.com/Peace_conference).

findings.title: The Korean War itself is the design spec: war aims are a discrete, priced ladder, and crossing a rung crosses a patron red line
findings.detail: US war aims in 1950 evolved through explicit, documented rungs: restore status quo ante (June) → destroy the NKPA → NSC-81/1 authorizing crossing the 38th parallel (approved Sept 11) → occupation and unification (October). Crossing the parallel was a deliberate decision that triggered Chinese intervention — and the intelligence failure around it (Acheson calling intervention 'sheer madness'; the community reading Chinese warnings as bluff) is precisely a fog-of-war/intel mechanic: the aggressor's ESTIMATE of the patron's red line, not the red line itself, drove the decision. UNGA Resolution 376 even gave unification temporary international legitimacy — legitimacy that evaporated once China entered. So the game should model war aims as declared, escalating rungs (upgrade = instant tension + shifted patron calculus), patron red lines as sharp hidden thresholds discoverable through espionage at varying confidence, and UN legitimacy as a resource you can secure in advance that decays when the war outgrows its mandate.
findings.evidence: [NSC-81/1 and the Evolution of U.S. War Aims in Korea (DTIC)](https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/tr/pdf/ADA378379.pdf), [Chinese intervention — Navy History](https://www.history.navy.mil/research/library/online-reading-room/title-list-alphabetically/n/new-equation.html), [FRUS 1950 vol. VII](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1950v07/comp4?start=301). The project's own docs/research/sovereignty-1950.md already catalogs the period's settlement vocabulary (trusteeships, four-power occupation, non-recognized annexation of the Baltics) — the menu below is drawn from it.

findings.title: Post-1945 norms make outright annexation the OUTLIER settlement, and the game's victory currency is the natural punisher
findings.detail: In the actual period, superpowers did not annex defeated states — the menu was occupation-then-restoration (Japan, Austria 1955), division (Germany, Korea), trusteeship (Somaliland, Libya per UNGA 289), and satellites. The one standing annexation on the 1950 map (the Baltics) was permanently non-recognized by the West — a status the project's sovereignty research explicitly preserved 'in case a non-recognized-annexation mechanic materializes'. That mechanic should materialize here: held-but-unrecognized territory is a durable, miserable state, not an error. And because UGS scores victory in bloc alignment, prestige, and avoided catastrophe (vision.md), annexation's true price can be paid in victory currency itself: neutral states drift toward the other bloc ('this is what they do to small nations' is free enemy propaganda), allies restrict basing, era checkpoints score you down. Maximal conquest trades the thing the game counts for map paint that the game does not count — possible, legal in the sim, and strategically self-defeating unless the player has pre-paid legitimacy and compensation. That is exactly the requested shape: possible but never free.
findings.evidence: docs/design/vision.md (era-scored victory, alignment/prestige); docs/research/sovereignty-1950.md items 4, 5, 8, 10 (Libya/Somalia trusteeships, Austria four-power occupation, Baltic non-recognition); Austrian State Treaty 1955 and San Francisco Treaty 1951 as the period's restoration-for-neutrality/alignment templates.

findings.title: Sharp thresholds where an actor decides; smooth curves where aggregates accumulate — and never guard a discrete prize with only a smooth cost
findings.detail: The genre's threshold failures are all cases of players surfing just below a line (49 AE, 99 infamy, tension 24.9) because the line was the ONLY cost. Rule: sharp thresholds belong where the fiction is a decision by an intelligent actor — patron intervention/consent, war-aim rungs, recognition (binary per country), tension bands — because decisions create brinkmanship and give espionage something to steal (where exactly is the line? how resolved are they?). Smooth curves belong where the fiction is accumulation — garrison drain scaling with occupied population, insurgency growth, integration progress, world-opinion drift — because smooth scaling makes small settlements naturally cheap with no special-casing (a 3-province DMZ adjustment rounds to noise; all of North Korea is a standing army's upkeep). The two must be layered: below every sharp threshold, a smooth cost so hovering still bleeds; behind every smooth curve, at least one threshold so the accumulation eventually MEANS something. UGS's existing tension design (integer tenths, named bands, era floor) already follows this pattern and should be the template.
findings.evidence: docs/design/systems/tension.md (bands + floor + decay structure); EU4/Vic3 threshold-surfing behavior per the forum sources above; Terra Invicta's cap-with-penalty-gradient as the layered model ([wiki](https://wiki.hoodedhorse.com/Terra_Invicta/Control_Point_Capacity)).

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Patron consent as the settlement gate (war ends by signature, not by button)
mechanics_recommendations.why: The master anti-exploit. 'Transfer all to me' stops being a button because no demand takes legal effect until every veto player — the enemy, its great-power patron(s), and (for UN-flagged wars) the UN sponsor bloc — accepts. Maximal demands mean the patron never signs, and an unsigned war keeps costing (garrisons, elevated tension floor, insurgency, war weariness). Consent cannot be timer-juggled, only earned, bought, or bypassed at explicit ongoing cost.
mechanics_recommendations.how: State: per-war `SettlementTable { demands: Vec<Demand>, veto_players: Vec<CountryTag>, acceptance: BTreeMap<CountryTag, i32> }`. Acceptance per veto player is an integer score: base from war exhaustion and battlefield position (line of control vs their red-line provinces), minus demand severity (each Demand has a severity cost in the vetoer's eyes, data-driven per relationship), plus compensation offered (concessions elsewhere: recognition, UN seat, base withdrawals, tech/trade — priced in influence and alignment), plus tension pressure (at Brink, everyone's acceptance rises — off-ramp seeking, matching the existing AI note in tension.md). Threshold at 0 = signs. Red-line demands (e.g. hostile troops on the Yalu, PRC) apply a large negative that compensation cannot fully offset unless the patron's army is broken. The player sees each vetoer's acceptance as an intel-quality-fuzzed range (reuse the war-legibility estimate rules: two significant figures, sampled per period), so espionage missions can narrow it — MacArthur's mistake as gameplay.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Declared war-aims ladder with priced rung upgrades
mechanics_recommendations.why: Prevents free demand-creep ('I'm here anyway, take it all'). NSC-81/1 as mechanic: escalating your aim mid-war is a discrete, visible, priced decision — instant tension, patron acceptance shifts, UN legitimacy consequences — made BEFORE you own the outcome, not at a spoils screen after.
mechanics_recommendations.how: State: per-war `WarAim` enum ladder, e.g. Repel → Punish (destroy army) → Occupy (regime change/unify) → Absorb (annex). Declaring at war start is cheap for Repel, and each upgrade is a `SimCommand` costing: instant tension (+10 to +25 tenths-scale per rung, tuning module), a UN-legitimacy delta (negative unless a UN resolution event pre-authorized the rung, as UNGA 376 did historically), and a recomputation of every vetoer's red-line check. Settlement demands are capped at your current declared aim — you can always settle for LESS than your aim (cheap, even tension-relieving) but never demand ABOVE it. AI patrons read aim upgrades as provocation triggers: upgrading to Occupy against a state on a patron's border rolls intervention logic that rung Repel never would.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Occupation burden: smooth garrison drain plus staged integration, forever until settled
mechanics_recommendations.why: The Terra Invicta lesson — capacity beats price. Holding land is a permanent bleed in currencies conquest does not replenish (stockpile, manpower, home consent), so even a 'won' maximal occupation competes with the arms race every month. Small settlements are automatically cheap because the curve scales with occupied population.
mechanics_recommendations.how: State: `Occupation { province, occupier, resistance: i32, status: Military|Trustee|Puppet|Integrating|Integrated }`. Monthly (`new_month`): garrison requirement = base + population/k, scaled by resistance; unmet requirement raises resistance and lets insurgency events fire. Garrison draws real manpower/stockpile from the existing pipeline (men in the OCCUPATION bucket are visibly not in FIELDED — conservation of mass per the war-legibility principles). Resistance grows smoothly, faster when the war is unsettled and faster still when a patron funds it covertly (an espionage-pillar op the AI actually runs: the USSR/PRC get a 'sponsor resistance' operation targeting unrecognized occupations, deniable, discoverable by counterintel). Integration (only after a signed settlement grants the land, or decades of unrecognized holding) is an investment project over years during which the territory produces at a small fraction. All constants in a `settlement::tuning` module.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Imposed peace as a real, punitive-but-playable state (non-recognition), with no truce shield
mechanics_recommendations.why: Closes the two classic exploits at once: the EU4 truce-shield (peace as protection you can time) and the current game's accidental version (hold everything forever, free). A player who won't pay for consent can walk away from the table — the game must not block it — but what they get is the Baltic-annexation status: held, unrecognized, contested.
mechanics_recommendations.how: A `SimCommand::ImposeSettlement` ends active hostilities without signatures. Effects: no truce — the enemy and patron may resume or proxy at any time; tension era floor rises (+50 tenths per major unrecognized occupation, feeding the existing era-floor hook in tension.md); occupation costs never taper and resistance sponsorship is always available to the patron; every country tracks `recognizes: bool` per transferred territory (BTreeMap, deterministic iteration), and unrecognized holdings apply a smooth ongoing penalty to alignment drift in the influence system — neutral and decolonizing states shift away from the occupier's bloc each month ('annexation propaganda'). Recognition arrives per-country via later settlement, compensation, or a slow generational normalization event chain (decades). Contrast: an AGREED settlement grants a hard truce, a large tension drop, and immediate legal status — making the signed path actively pleasant, not just less bad.

mechanics_recommendations.mechanic: Settlement menu with per-line-item, multi-currency price tags shown before demanding
mechanics_recommendations.why: Civ 5's opacity is the legibility failure to avoid; Civ 6's grievances show legible per-actor costs work. The player must be able to read, at the table, exactly what each end-state costs in tension, UN standing, influence/compensation, and projected occupation upkeep — so choosing 'new DMZ' over 'unify' is an informed strategic trade, not a guess.
mechanics_recommendations.how: UI (app crate) renders the sim's `SettlementTable`: rows for status-quo-ante, border adjustment, demilitarized buffer, neutralization (Austria model: unify/restore in exchange for no bases/alliances — costs the strategic asset, buys patron consent), UN trusteeship (shared cost, shared legitimacy, later supervised elections resolved by the influence pillar), puppet, unification-under-client, annexation. Each row shows: instant tension delta (relief for de-escalatory rows), UN legitimacy delta, compensation the vetoers would require (computed from acceptance shortfall), and projected monthly occupation cost from the burden formulas. Vetoer acceptance per row shown as a fuzzed gauge. This is one deterministic pure function over existing state — no new randomness.

pitfalls: Paying the penalty in a currency the conquest replenishes (EU4's wide-is-right): if occupied Korea's industry offsets its own garrison cost, or war spoils fund the compensation that buys consent, the stack collapses. Occupation must drain currencies land does not produce — legitimacy, patron goodwill, home-front manpower/consent — and occupied territory must produce near-nothing until legally integrated.

Time as the universal solvent (Vic3 infamy): if tension, non-recognition, and resistance all fade on a clock, the strategy becomes 'annex, idle at speed 5, repeat'. Decay must be conditional — recognition requires acts, resistance falls only under adequate garrison AND settlement, the tension era floor stays raised while occupations are unrecognized.

Peace-as-shield exploits (EU4 truce juggling): any protection window granted by an imposed or minimal peace becomes a timing tool. Only fully-signed settlements grant truces; imposed ones grant none, and patrons must be willing to re-enter or proxy while terms are unsigned.

Over-deterrence (the Vic3 'game says no' complaint, Civ's eternal warmonger mark): if every settlement stings, players read the system as anti-fun railroading. Small settlements must be actively rewarding — status quo ante gives tension relief, prestige, and UN standing — so the menu reads as strategy, not punishment; and defender/aggressor asymmetry must be explicit (repelling an invasion carries no stigma).

Veto players as scripted walls: if PRC consent is an opaque, immovable 'no', the negotiation is railroading with extra steps. Red lines must be intel-discoverable (with confidence levels), genuinely movable by compensation and battlefield state, and occasionally wrong in the player's estimate — the MacArthur failure should be reproducible by a player with bad intel, and that is a feature.

Sharp thresholds with no smooth cost beneath them invite surfing (49.9-tension play, one-province-under-the-line annexations): every threshold needs a gradient under it, every gradient needs a threshold above it.
analysts.korea_test: Situation: USA (UN flag) occupies all of North Korea, holds the Yalu; PRC engaged, USSR patron in the background. War aim was upgraded to Occupy/Unify when the player crossed the parallel (instant tension hit already paid; UN legitimacy intact only if the UNGA-376-style resolution event was secured first). The settlement table now shows, with PRC and USSR as veto players and their acceptance gauges intel-fuzzed: (1) STATUS QUO ANTE — withdraw to the 38th: PRC/USSR accept immediately, large tension relief, UN prestige gain, minor domestic hawk backlash; the cheap, historical-armistice-shaped exit. (2) NEW LINE at the peninsula's neck (Pyongyang–Wonsan): acceptable to the PRC only with a demilitarized band and no US troops near the Yalu; modest tension cost, small permanent garrison; the 'better DMZ' alt-history. (3) NEUTRALIZED UNIFIED KOREA (Austria 1955 model): unification granted in exchange for no US bases or alliance — PRC acceptance reachable with moderate compensation; the player wins the map but forfeits the strategic asset; a genuinely interesting trade. (4) UN TRUSTEESHIP of the north: shared garrison cost, legitimacy preserved, supervised elections in ~5 years whose outcome is decided by the influence pillar — the war becomes an influence contest. (5) UNIFICATION UNDER SEOUL with US alliance: hard PRC red line while US forces stand on the Yalu; acceptance requires either breaking the Chinese expeditionary army at Brink-band tension with the USSR declining to back them (an intel question the player can research and get WRONG), or enormous compensation (PRC UN seat, Taiwan-strait withdrawal, recognition) priced in influence the player may not have; expensive but reachable — the alt-history the player asked for, never free. (6) ANNEXATION by the USA: no vetoer ever signs; available only via ImposeSettlement — no truce (PRC free to resume, USSR runs MiG-Alley-style deniable support and funds a northern insurgency through the espionage system), tension era floor permanently raised, ~150k-man garrison drawn visibly out of the FIELDED bucket every month, occupied provinces produce almost nothing while unrecognized, and every neutral and decolonizing state drifts eastward monthly as 'America annexes nations' propaganda compounds — the player converts the game's actual victory currencies (alignment, prestige, avoided catastrophe at era checkpoints) into map paint. Meanwhile the AI: PRC keeps probing while unsigned; USSR compensates globally; UN allies peel contributions once the war outgrows the mandate they endorsed. Every option exists, the extreme ones are priced in consent and permanent bleed rather than blocked, and the cheap options are genuinely rewarding — no single 'win the war get everything' button anywhere in the stack.

principles.principle: 1. Wars are fought FOR declared, visible war aims — a discrete ladder revisable mid-war only as a priced, provocative act. Demands at settlement are capped at the current declared aim; upgrading the aim (crossing the 38th) is itself the escalation event that shifts patron calculus.
principles.support: HoI4 analyst (missing war-aims concept is the root architectural flaw), Paradox lens (declared aims as the spine; CK3/Vic3 evidence), anti-exploit (NSC-81/1 rung ladder with priced upgrades and demand cap), alt-history (ambition priced at demand time, Vic3 infamy insight), both historians (NSC-81/1 as the historical war-aims document).

principles.principle: 2. Termination is a process that runs DURING the war, never a post-victory conference screen. Talks open at a willingness threshold (the existing armistice trigger, repurposed); the front line at signature is the settlement line, so late offensives are bargaining moves.
principles.support: All seven. HoI4 analyst (the terminal minigame is the thing to avoid), Paradox lens (settlement table replacing auto-armistice), cold-war-historian (Panmunjom: 2 years of fighting-while-talking, 45% of US casualties after talks opened), alt-history (real-time negotiation, not a modal), occupation-mechanics (settlement generator at armistice), anti-exploit, occupation-historian.

principles.principle: 3. Patron consent is the master gate and the master anti-exploit. Every war's stakeholder set is belligerents ∪ patrons ∪ (UN if mandated). Clauses touching a client's existence require its patron to sign, be defeated, or be verifiably distracted — and patrons receive concessions, never territory. A veto held by a live AI actor cannot be timer-juggled the way a numeric penalty can.
principles.support: All seven, independently and emphatically. HoI4 analyst (patron veto), Paradox lens (patron pressure term), cold-war-historian (Suez/Tashkent/1973: decisive pressure flows patron-to-client), occupation-historian ('negotiating only with the defeated' named as a pitfall), alt-history (patron-consent gate), anti-exploit ('consent held by an AI actor is not a speed bump').

principles.principle: 4. Recognition is a persistent per-country status, not a one-time price. Signed settlements grant recognition (truce, tension release, legal ownership); unilateral changes stay unrecognized and bleed FOREVER — tension floor, neutral-alignment drift, rival-funded insurgency, near-zero production — until discharged by acts (later settlement, compensation, generational events), never by idle time.
principles.support: HoI4 analyst (recognition layer; one-time prices always get paid), occupation-historian (Baltic non-recognition as the era's actual mechanism: 'delegitimize, don't price'), anti-exploit (Vic3 time-decay failure; no truce shield on imposed peace), Paradox lens (treaty objects with per-signatory recognition flags), alt-history (FrozenConflict/unrecognized aftermath objects).

principles.principle: 5. No fungible war-score currency. Settlement costs are convex in distance-from-status-quo and denominated in multiple NON-CONVERTIBLE currencies: military position buys lines, patron consent buys sovereignty transfers, legitimacy buys recognition, and tension/alignment are costs paid rather than resources spent. Status quo ante is near-free and actively rewarding.
principles.support: HoI4 analyst (fungible score produced the shopping sprees), Paradox lens (multi-channel costs vs the 49-AE cliff meta), occupation-mechanics (prohibitive costs must be non-fungible), alt-history (convex W^1.5 pricing, heterogeneous currencies), anti-exploit (never pay the penalty in a currency conquest replenishes).

principles.principle: 6. Occupation is live, expensive state between armistice and settlement — zone-level (1-3 zones per war, never per-province), two tracks (military control vs population alignment), one policy posture per zone, with the garrison drawn from the REAL army pool so pacification competes with the front line.
principles.support: occupation-mechanics (COIN control/support split, Vietnam '65 shared pool, anti-micromanagement lesson), HoI4 analyst (La Resistance engine, finally wired to peace pricing), occupation-historian (authority + upkeep + multi-year consolidation clocks), anti-exploit (capacity beats price; occupied land produces near-nothing until legally integrated), alt-history (OccupationAuthority object).

Resistance level in your occupied zone is partly a dial held by your rival (a covert-ops budget line), which makes it negotiable (settlements can cut the tap) and gives counterintel a job. Without a sponsor it decays into an ignorable tax.

principles.principle: 8. The frozen conflict — armistice without treaty — is first-class content, not a failure state. It is the era's signature outcome (Korea 1953, Kashmir, the Golan) and the natural fallback when patron consent is unreachable: line fixed, claims unresolved, DMZ upkeep, tension floor, a standing 'convene conference' action re-evaluated as the world changes.
