synthesis.shape:
THE ARCHITECTURE — five layers, all in ugs-sim, all deterministic.

**Layer 1: War Aims.** Every war carries per-belligerent declared aims from a small closed ladder: `Repel/StatusQuoAnte` (defender's free default, always) → `Punish` (break the enemy army) → `NewLine(Vec<ProvinceId>)` → `Unify/RegimeChange(under: CountryTag)`. There is no `Absorb` rung for whole states — border adjustments yes, absorbing a Korea/Germany-class state into the victor, no (the occupation-historian's strongest finding; wholesale absorption happens only through the unilateral-hold path below, which is never a signable clause). Upgrading an aim is a `SimCommand`: instant tension delta (tuning module), political-will cost, UN-legitimacy delta (negative unless a resolution event pre-authorized it), and a recompute of every patron's red-line check — crossing the 38th mechanically CAUSES the intervention risk the game already models. Settlement demands are capped at your current aim; you can always settle for less (cheap, tension-relieving), never demand more.

**Layer 2: The Settlement Table.** A per-war `SettlementTable` entity, open from the moment the existing armistice-willingness trigger fires (repurposed as 'talks open', not 'war ends'), evaluated monthly in `TickSet::Politics` off `SimClock::new_month`, RNG via `rng.fork(b"settlement")`. Proposals are bundles of clauses from a closed enum — `BorderChange(line)`, `DMZ(provinces, depth)`, `Neutralization(country)`, `Trusteeship(admin, review_date)`, `ClientState(tag, autonomy)`, `Unification(under)`, `Recognition(change)`, `Reparations`, later `POWRepatriation(mode)` — with named historical templates in RON (`status_quo_ante`, `new_dmz`, `neutralized_unification`, `un_trusteeship`, `unification_south`, ...) so the AI can evaluate packages and the player gets legibility, while the clause grammar keeps hybrids emergent.

Acceptance per stakeholder (belligerents ∪ patrons ∪ UN-flag) is deterministic integer math with three independent hard gates on top of a utility comparison: (1) MILITARY — territorial clauses only offerable over territory occupied or within a narrow band of the line of control; (2) PATRON — sovereignty-transferring clauses against a client require the patron's signature, or the patron defeated/distracted past a threshold; red-line demands (hostile forces on the Yalu) apply a penalty compensation cannot fully offset while the patron's army stands; (3) LEGITIMACY — high-sovereignty-weight clauses spend legitimacy earned from UN resolutions and coalition breadth. Utility: U_settle vs U_continue = expected line shift − exhaustion rate − escalation risk. Pricing is convex: clause sovereignty weights sum to W, tension cost ∝ W^1.5, so unification costs ~8× a border tweak. Every row of every stakeholder's ledger is visible; the stakeholder's resolve/red-line position is shown as an intel-quality-fuzzed range that espionage ops narrow. Patrons never bid for territory — they take concessions (recognition, seats, base withdrawals, trade) and can coerce their own clients (arms cutoff, financial squeeze, guarantee packages: the Suez/Rhee toolkit, v2).

**Layer 3: Occupation.** Replaces the frozen province→occupier map with 1-3 `OccupationZone`s per war (occupied North Korea is ONE zone). Each zone: `control` (0-100, set by garrison ratio vs insurgency), `alignment` (-100..100, moved slowly by policy, war conduct, sponsor pressure), and one policy posture — MilitaryGovernment / ClientAdministration / Trusteeship / Exploitation — trading across different currencies (garrison manpower vs money vs tension vs alliance cohesion) so no posture dominates. Garrison requirement = f(population, insurgency, policy) drawn from the REAL army pool: divisions on occupation duty are visibly absent from the front. Monthly upkeep drains the treasury; occupied land produces near-nothing until legally integrated (anti-exploit: conquest must not fund its own penalty). Insurgency per zone is fed by (100−alignment), border porosity (sanctuary adjacency — the Yalu is maximally porous), and a sponsor tap: a covert budget line rivals fund through the existing espionage v1 machinery, suppressed by garrisons and counterintel, occasionally flaring into events that demand decisions — never generic rebel stacks, never a pure attrition tax.

**Layer 4: Outcomes as objects.** Three terminal shapes, all stable and playable. (a) SIGNED SETTLEMENT: executes transfers, creates puppets/DMZs/trusteeships as entities, grants a hard truce and per-signatory recognition, schedules future events (plebiscite in N months, resolved by the influence pillar), releases tension, ends occupation drain. (b) ARMISTICE WITHOUT TREATY (the existing mechanic, upgraded): creates a `FrozenConflict` — MDL + DMZ province strip, garrison requirements both sides, tension floor, RevanchistClaim on the loser, and a standing convene-conference action whose gates re-evaluate monthly as the world changes. (c) UNILATERAL HOLD (`ImposeSettlement`): ends shooting without signatures — NO truce, permanently unrecognized holdings tracked in a per-country `recognizes` BTreeMap, raised tension era floor, monthly neutral-alignment drift against the occupier, standing sponsor-funded insurgency, production near zero. Recognition discharges only through acts: later settlements, compensation, or systemic generational events — never idle time.

**Layer 5: Pressure and shocks.** Per-belligerent `PoliticalWill` pool (government-type-asymmetric drain from casualties, duration, occupation, refusing ledger-reasonable offers; restored by achieving declared aims) feeds acceptance and domestic events — soft pressure only, never a forced peace on the player. Deadlocks break via systemic shocks, not scripts: leadership-transition risk (Stalin's-death analog from `rng.fork(b"succession")` against age/stability tables), elections, and escalation events; direct superpower contact or a nuclear alert spawns a compressed forced-termination sequence in which patrons impose the current line on AI clients — the player-as-client may refuse at the cost of severing patronage.

**Pillar service.** Escalation: aim upgrades, red lines, W^1.5 tension pricing, the compression clock. Ideology/influence: legitimacy, alignment drift against unrecognized occupiers, plebiscites and trusteeship elections decided by influence. Intelligence: red-line discovery, sponsor-resistance ops and counterintel, collaboration prep lowering settlement costs. Economy: occupation upkeep vs the arms race, compensation packages, embargo pressure from non-recognizers. The limited-war thesis is enforced structurally: restraint (status quo ante) is rewarded, ambition is continuously priced from declaration, and maximal outcomes cost the game's actual victory currencies.

tensions.tension: Is wholesale annexation on the menu at all? Both historians argue it should simply not be a settlement clause (no 1945-90 precedent; 'not on the menu IS the design statement'), while the HoI4, Paradox, anti-exploit, and alt-history analysts want it possible-but-ruinous per the player's own requirement.
tensions.recommendation: Both, split by path: no signable clause ever offers absorbing a whole state into the victor (border adjustments and client-state clauses are the ceiling of the table), but the unilateral path — ImposeSettlement / just keep holding — always exists and produces the Baltic-annexation status: permanently unrecognized, no truce, bleeding on every channel. Annexation is possible as a fait accompli the world never accepts, exactly matching both the history and the 'possible but never free' brief.

tensions.tension: Legibility vs min-maxing. Most analysts demand a fully visible deterministic acceptance ledger; the cold-war-historian warns that readable timers get min-maxed and that real deadlocks broke via unpredictable shocks (Stalin's death), not smooth attrition.
tensions.recommendation: Split structure from timing. The ledger's STRUCTURE is fully visible (which clause is blocked, by whom, by which gate, and what would flip it); the opponent's resolve, red-line positions, and shock timing are fuzzed/unknowable — red lines shown as intel-confidence ranges, deadlock-breaking shocks driven by systemic probability (succession tables, elections) the player can see as risk factors but not schedule. Refusal is a puzzle; the break date is not.

tensions.tension: Negotiation granularity: the cold-war-historian wants multi-agenda-item conferences where non-territorial items (POWs, foreign-force withdrawal, table shape) deadlock independently for months; other analysts model a single bundled proposal with one acceptance score per stakeholder.
tensions.recommendation: V1 ships the bundled-proposal model — it delivers the whole strategic layer with far less machinery. Design the clause enum so non-territorial items (POWRepatriation, ForeignForceWithdrawal) slot in later as high-stubbornness clauses that can individually stall a package. Add them in v2 for pacing texture; do not block the v1 slice on them.

tensions.tension: Client obstruction: the cold-war-historian makes the Rhee/Thieu loop (your OWN ally sabotaging the peace, bought off with defense treaties or removed by covert op) central; most other analysts omit it entirely.
tensions.recommendation: Defer the full obstruction loop (sabotage events, Everready covert-removal, guarantee packages) to v2, but include clients in the stakeholder set from day one with their own aims and a visible dissatisfaction readout — per the historian's own caveat, obstruction should degrade and complicate settlements, never hard-wall them (the US signed at Panmunjom without Rhee). The data model must not need rework to add it.

tensions.tension: Hard clocks: the historian wants a ForcedTermination sequence (patrons impose terms within days when superpowers touch); the Paradox analyst's strongest pitfall is any forced peace that overrides a winning player (Stellaris).
tensions.recommendation: Forced termination applies fully to AI clients — that is historically right and makes patron leverage real. The PLAYER as client is presented the imposition and may refuse, at severe explicit cost: patronage severed, aid cut, alliance cohesion collapse, political-will hemorrhage. Agency is never confiscated; refusing your superpower is simply one of the most expensive decisions in the game.

tensions.tension: Occupation track count: occupation-mechanics insists on two tracks (control vs alignment, the COIN lesson); occupation-historian's model uses a single 'authority' value plus time-gated disposition clocks.
tensions.recommendation: Keep two tracks. The single-authority model cannot express 'militarily quiet but politically hostile', which is the precise state that should gate the good outcomes (plebiscite, client legitimacy) versus the cheap ones (raw control). synthesis.korea_acid_test:
January 1951, alt-history: the US holds every North Korean province, the PLA glowers across the Yalu. The war carries a UN mandate; the player upgraded aims to Unify when crossing the 38th, paying tension then. The map is no longer frozen — occupied North Korea is one OccupationZone (control climbing, alignment poor under ROK administration, insurgency fed by a maximally porous Chinese border), garrison demand pins four to six divisions the Yalu line wants, and monthly upkeep runs. The Settlement Table is open, PRC and USSR sitting as veto players with intel-fuzzed acceptance gauges.

The menu, priced: (1) STATUS QUO ANTE — withdraw to the 38th. W=0: PRC/USSR accept within a month or two, large tension release, UN prestige gain, political-will recovery for achieving the original defensive aim, modest hawk backlash at home. The cheap, dignified, historical exit — and it feels like a win. (2) NEW LINE at the Pyongyang–Wonsan neck plus a DMZ clause. Offerable because occupied; PRC acceptance goes positive only as its offensives fail and its will drains — months of fighting-while-talking, the line sampled at signature, so the PLA keeps pushing to bend it. Produces a Treaty, a rump revanchist DPRK, a DMZ entity, and permanent garrison upkeep. (3) UN TRUSTEESHIP over the North — legitimacy-priced rather than tension-priced: occupation costs shared, tension drops, supervised elections scheduled ~24 months out and decided by the influence pillar, which rival covert ops can sabotage. The patient player's route. (4) NEUTRALIZED UNIFIED KOREA (the Austria lever): the Unification clause paired with Neutralization — no US bases, no alliance — collapses the patron penalty; Moscow and Beijing sign for moderate compensation. The player wins the map and forfeits the strategic asset. (5) UNIFICATION UNDER THE ROK with US alliance: all three gates bind. Military — survive the standing Chinese counterblow; patron — a hard PRC red line while US forces sit on the Yalu, offsettable only by enormous compensation (recognition, UN seat, strait concessions) or a systemic key: Soviet succession crisis, a Moscow-consuming crisis elsewhere, or brinkmanship raising THEIR escalation risk — each dangerous, and the player's read of the red line is intel-fuzzed, so the MacArthur miscalculation is reproducible. Even signed, it spawns years of OccupationAuthority in the North: PRC-funded insurgency, garrison bills, a militarized Yalu tension floor. (6) UNILATERAL HOLD: no annexation clause exists; the player may simply impose. No truce — the PLA can resume at will; every holding unrecognized; tension era floor rises; neutrals drift toward Moscow monthly on annexation propaganda; the North produces nothing; the USSR runs deniable air support and a sponsored insurgency through the espionage layer. Sustainable only as a bleeding strategic choice.

Meanwhile the world acts: PRC intervention posture scales with non-ROK divisions in Yalu border provinces (garrisoning the border with ROK units is playing the NSC-81/1 constraint correctly); the ROK's own aim is Unify, so every lesser package accrues visible client dissatisfaction (v2: sabotage events); allies pressure for settlement as the war outgrows the mandate; and refusing a ledger-reasonable offer drains US political will monthly. If talks deadlock, the fallback is the armistice the player already has — now a FrozenConflict that ticks costs on both sides forever, which is precisely what history did. Every requested alt-history is reachable; nothing, including doing nothing, is free.
